author: Julius Gavroche
title: World of Hurt
content:
Abolitionist Reflections on the Root Causes of Harm




from the 

CrimethInc.

 collective, 17/11/2026




What causes people to harm others? Reactionaries label certain individuals—or, worse, entire demographics—inherently harmful to justify their own efforts to inflict harm via vigilante attacks, policing, and the court system. Others suggest that experiencing harm can lead some to harm others, as suggested by the common catchphrase “

Hurt people hurt people

.” Here, we examine this popular notion and propose a more useful framework for understanding the root causes of harm.




Today, a ruling class headed by billionaires and aspiring autocrats is making 

the celebration of violence

 central to their narratives and policies, openly campaigning against empathy itself. In this context, the question of what causes harm—and how to interrupt it without reinforcing cycles of suffering and oppression—has become increasingly urgent.










World of Hurt




Abolitionists

 who envision a world without 

police

 or 

prisons

 often face questions about how to address serious forms of interpersonal harm. 

Mutual aid

 and resource redistribution may reduce behaviors that arise as a consequence of lack of access to basic needs. But how can we understand those who seem to hurt others out of cruelty or disregard? If we don’t accept the idea that some people are monsters who must be locked up to keep the rest of us safe, how can we make sense of their actions?




Defenders of the criminal legal system frequently cite rape and abuse to justify prisons and imprisonment. In response, abolitionists have devoted considerable energy to developing 

alternative approaches

 to addressing sexual violence. Groups such as Generation Five have proposed 

principles for responding to child sexual abuse

 through transformative justice frameworks. By focusing on one of the most stigmatized forms of harm, they aim to cut to the root of 

carceral thinking

 in order to reimagine safety and justice.




But creative responses beyond the state are not enough. To end sexual violence, we also need to understand its root causes.




Feminist activists coined the term “

rape culture

” to describe how social norms and institutions enable sexual harm. In addition to these structural effects of gender and power, others argue that past experiences of harm shape the behavior of individuals who go on to harm others. One of the most common ways to articulate this principle appears in the phrase “

Hurt people hurt people

.”




Let’s take a closer look to see where this popular saying came from, how it is used, and its implications for an abolitionist understanding of harm.













The Trajectory of a Slogan




From 

self-help books

 and 

therapist blogs

 to the 

writings of abolitionist activists

, “hurt people hurt people” has become an influential account of the psychology of violence. It suggests that some people harm others not because they are pathological monsters, but because they too are victims whose unresolved trauma shapes their hurtful actions.




The precise origins of the phrase are opaque, but it has been in circulation 

at least since the 1950s

. It seems to have begun trending in the 1990s in therapeutic and pop psychology circles. A popular 1993 Christian self-help book titled 

Hurt People Hurt People

 promised to support readers in healing from painful past relationships “with empathy and biblical insight.” In recent years, this phrase has been repeated by everyone from megachurch pastor Rick Warren to Hollywood actor Andrew Garfield to the stripper con artist character Destiny in the movie 

Hustlers

 to 

the metal band Mudvayne

. It appears most widely in discourse about therapy, self-help, trauma, and religion.




On the surface, “hurt people hurt people” might seem an odd slogan for radical critics of the 

prison industrial complex

. As a maxim of folk wisdom that spans mainstream, religious, feminist, and radical circles, we should consider carefully whether it aligns with our values.




In some ways, it makes sense that abolitionists would find this formulation promising. It humanizes people who cause harm, whereas dehumanizing them paves the way for carceral responses. It attributes the roots of harmful behavior not to inherent depravity, but to contingent circumstances that can be changed. It resonates with the lived experiences of some people who are struggling to heal and to be accountable for hurting others. It seems to offer a hopeful pathway towards a world without sexual violence by intervening in support of those who have been harmed in order to interrupt the cycle.




This compassionate approach to rethinking the causes of violence has inspired abolitionist activists such as 

Mariame Kaba

. In her book 

We Do This ’Til We Free Us: Abolitionist Organizing and Transforming Justice

, she discusses transformative justice alternatives to criminal punishment. Following an instance of harm, she writes, we should first center the immediate needs of a survivor. Next, however, she argues that







We would also focus on the person responsible for the harm—but without disregarding their humanity. This means we have to acknowledge the reality that often it is hurt people who hurt other people. Understanding that harm originates from situations dominated by stress, scarcity, and oppression, one way to prevent violence is to make sure that people have support to get the things they need.







Kaba considers both power structures and individual psychology in responding to violence. Her book proposes a pathway toward the prevention of harm through community support and trauma resolution rather than punishment.




Other abolitionist writers and activists have taken up the phrase. In a chapter on “Healing as Abolitionist Practice,” the authors of 

Thinking Like an Abolitionist to End Sexual Violence in Higher Education

 recount the story of a person who was sexually assaulted by a friend who was himself a survivor of child sexual abuse.




“In reflecting on her trauma,” the authors explain, the young woman interpreted the experience through the lens of “‘hurt people hurt people’—a concept that rings true for her own experiences as someone who has harmed as well.” Having both experienced and caused harm in intimate relationships herself, she decided to turn away from carceral responses. Instead, she pursued a pathway to accountability with the person who had harmed her, intending not to punish him but to reduce the likelihood that he would harm others in the future. The authors cited this framework in their discussions about abolition and sexual violence on college campuses.




Yet despite these positive examples, “hurt people hurt people” poses problems that should prompt abolitionists to reconsider using it. The slogan risks reinforcing victim-blaming and misunderstanding the root causes of harm. Let’s dig deeper and look for an alternative framework to recognize pathways to change while more accurately analyzing the origins of sexual violence.













The Problem with “Hurt People Hurt People”




What’s wrong with the idea that “hurt people hurt people”?




Consider: in general, which people experience the most harm in our society? 

Oppressed people

. Who is primarily responsible for that harm? 

Their oppressors

.




Of course, we know that oppressed people hurt others in many ways. But Black people are not responsible for anti-Black racism; white people, and sometimes other non-Black people, are. Trans people are not responsible for transphobia; cis people are. Posing “hurt people hurt people” as a totalizing explanation risks misrepresenting the root causes of harm and misattributing responsibility for it.




Yes, oppressors themselves have often been hurt in various ways, and are sometimes oppressed along other axes. For instance, white women often perpetuate racial oppression while experiencing gender oppression. There are countless such examples.




But is that what 

leads them

 to hurt others? If so, this framework seems to imply that as we go upwards in 

the pyramid of social power

, to levels where people are less and less oppressed, we should find people who hurt others less and less.




In fact, the opposite is true. To name a single example, Donald Trump’s widely exercised capacity to hurt others exceeds that of almost anyone in human history. However much he may have been hurt by others himself, the harm he causes stems directly from the sense of entitlement that his wealth, whiteness, maleness, US citizenship, and other aspects of privilege have bestowed upon him.




Perhaps, then, we need a more expansive sense of what it means to be “hurt.” From a certain perspective, 

white people are harmed by white supremacy

, which leaves them disconnected from ancestral cultures and land, with a truncated humanity and an inability to relate across lines of difference. Of course, they are hurt by white supremacy differently and far 

less

 severely than non-white people are. Likewise, 

men suffer under patriarchy

—experiencing rigidity, emotional disconnection, shorter lifespans, and greater likelihood of dying in battle—though certainly far 

less

 than women and trans men do. Can the “hurts” that privileged people experience account for their harmful actions?




It’s both accurate and politically strategic to emphasize the stake that 

all

 people have in dismantling systems of oppression, regardless of whether they are privileged or oppressed. If patriarchy is genuinely 

good for men

, if white supremacy is 

in the interest of white people

, then the only basis for men or white people to act against racism or sexism—to act 

against

 their interests—would be altruism or false consciousness. Self-sacrificing altruism alone will not suffice to move large numbers of men and white people to resist patriarchy and white supremacy, but the participation of millions of such people will almost certainly be necessary for us to dismantle those systems.




The 

well-known words of Lilla Watson and other Aboriginal Australian activists

 bear repeating here: “

If you have come here to help me, you are wasting your time. But if you have come because your liberation is bound up with mine, then let us work together

.” Describing the harms that systems of oppression do to those they privilege—as well as to those they oppress, if unequally—can form one strategy for promoting solidarity. But it may prove more valuable to emphasize, as the above quote does, a positive vision of mutually intertwined liberation.




Still, recognizing that both the privileged and the oppressed are “hurt” by systems of oppression doesn’t necessarily get us any closer to understanding the root causes of harm. It’s inaccurate and offensive to group these vastly different harms under a single generic category of “hurt.” And it makes little sense to attribute responsibility for the oppressive behaviors of members of dominant social groups to the “hurt” they supposedly experience as a consequence of occupying those dominant positions. On the contrary, it seems far more plausible that it is precisely the ways in which such people are 

not

 hurt—their privilege and entitlement—that facilitate their harmful behavior towards others.




These are good reasons to be suspicious of the “hurt people hurt people” framework. Nonetheless, it resonates deeply with many individuals, particularly in the sphere of intimate relationships. Could it still offer a transformative account of the causes of sexual violence?













Beneath the Statistics: How the Criminal Legal System Creates More Harm




Abolitionists reject the idea that some people are inherently, irredeemably bad and therefore deserve punishment and confinement. Instead, we seek to understand the root causes of harmful behavior. If people hurt others because they have themselves been hurt, then harmful behavior emerges from particular circumstances, circumstances that can be changed.




Many “crimes,” such as theft or trespassing, can easily be traced to unmet material needs. To reduce or eliminate these, we need to change our social system to ensure that everyone has access to food, housing, and other basic necessities. But more harmful behaviors such as assault or rape, which can’t be easily explained as people trying to meet core material needs, pose a deeper challenge to abolitionist logics.




Proposing that “hurt people hurt people” offers the hope that by interrupting cycles of harm, we can reduce the likelihood of hurt people in turn hurting others. By promoting healing, resolving trauma, and intervening to prevent harm, we can create a virtuous cycle in which hurt no longer creates more hurt. As fewer people experience sexual violence—the logic goes—fewer people hurt by that violence will hurt others in turn. As the prevalence of rape and abuse diminishes, the perceived need for carceral responses to it will diminish along with it.




Yet once again, the “hurt people hurt people” framing proves problematic when it comes to explaining sexual harm.




At first glance, research into sexual offenders appears to support a connection between experiencing sexual harm and causing it. Sexual violence advocates 

cite a range of studies

 claiming that “perpetrators of child sexual abuse are also often victims of child sexual abuse.

”

 As 

one 2014 study

 concluded, “Sex offenders had more than three times the odds of child sexual abuse, nearly twice the odds of physical abuse, thirteen times the odds of verbal abuse, and more than four times the odds of emotional neglect” relative to men in the general population.




On the surface, this appears to confirm that “hurt people hurt people” when it comes to sexual harm. However, a closer look through an abolitionist lens undermines this conclusion.




According to the criminal legal system’s 

own statistics

, “Rape is the most under-reported crime,” with at least 63% of sexual assaults not reported to police. That’s almost certainly a low figure, given how many survivors don’t define their non-consensual experiences as rape or may not report them on Department of Justice surveys. Additionally, in the minority of experiences of sexual assault that are reported to police, almost none result in convictions and fewer still in imprisonment. According to 

FBI statistics

, “For every 1000 sexual assaults, 50 reports lead to arrests, 28 cases lead to a felony conviction, and only 25 perpetrators are sentenced to incarceration.”




This means that the vast majority of people who commit sexual harm never end up in prison, so never end up in the statistics cited to claim that “hurt people hurt people.”




Who 

actually

 gets sent to prison for sexual offenses? It’s certainly not a representative sample of those who sexually harm others. It’s mostly people who are already vulnerable to the criminal legal system, often due to poverty, racism, and other forms of marginalization.




So when these statistics imply that “perpetrators” (in this case, the tiny percentage of people 

convicted and imprisoned

, not all people who 

commit

 such harms) are themselves disproportionately survivors of sexual abuse, what does that actually tell us?




It tells us that the people who are most likely to be caught up in the criminal legal system are the people who are most likely to be abused. Statistically, 

hurt people are

 

more likely to be hurt by the criminal legal system themselves

 than to hurt others. Consider the enormous proportion of 

incarcerated women who are survivors of partner violence

, whose “crime” was often simply survival.




The reality behind the statistics is that carceral responses are more likely to compound the harms that survivors experience than to prevent future harm or secure “justice.”













The Impact on Survivors




Beyond debates over statistics, there are additional problems with the framework “hurt people hurt people.” Let’s start with the impact it has on survivors themselves.




Consider this account 

from a rape crisis counselor

:







I began to reconsider this idea that “hurt people hurt people” when I worked as a facilitator for support groups of adult male survivors of child sexual abuse. One of the most painful feelings I heard these men express was the fear that they themselves might be doomed to hurt others because of what they’d experienced. This sentiment was frequently shared and widely resonant among the men in my groups. Many of them seemed to have absorbed the narrative that those who commit sexual abuse usually had been subjected to it themselves. They had no desire to hurt anyone; on the contrary, they had an absolute horror of making anyone go through what they had gone through. But they were terrified that somehow, because of what they’d experienced, they were at risk of causing harm to others. Some avoided intimate relationships or raising children because of these fears.







Despite the lingering power of this myth, the research that has been conducted indicates that it isn’t true. 

The National Sexual Violence Resource Center cautions

, “

IT IS RARE

 for victims of child sexual abuse to become perpetrators as adults.” They cite 

a 2015 study

 that concluded, “The widespread belief that sexually abused children are uniquely at risk to become sex offenders was not supported by prospective empirical evidence.”




Yet despite the lack of evidence, this myth remains deeply entrenched, in part due to the influence of the “hurt people hurt people” framework, which is often repeated by well-meaning abolitionists.




This myth inflicts a cruel additional punishment on survivors already burdened by the trauma they have experienced. It builds on the shame that survivors often feel, even when they know that the violence they endured wasn’t their fault. They often feel damaged or broken, and the myth that they are likely to go on to hurt others seems to confirm this. For this reason alone, we should consider the costs of reinforcing this paradigm.




This fear is also distinctly gendered. Female survivors are far less likely than male survivors to internalize the idea that experiencing rape or sexual abuse will lead them to harm others sexually. This is partly due to the social reality that men commit the greatest proportion of sexual violence. But it’s further reinforced by the relative invisibility of male survivors—and particularly for queer men, it’s compounded by the homophobic messaging that associates same-sex love with pedophilia.




Repeating the story that hurt people hurt people turns away from the feminist analysis of rape as an expression of power. In its place, we’re left with a depoliticized take on trauma that ignores how norms of gender and sexuality shape victimization and reinforce stigma.













Harm and Disrupted Empathy




If the framework “hurt people hurt people” does not offer an adequate explanation of the causes of oppression and abuse, what could be a useful alternative?




Here’s a different way that abolitionists might frame the roots of harm:




People with disrupted empathy hurt people.




Empathy here means our ability to perceive, understand, and respond to the feelings of others. It involves entering into another person’s reality, sensing their perspective and their emotions, and reshaping our actions based on that awareness. Empathy is the basis for human connection, a key foundation for relationships and communication. When it is disrupted, it undermines that connection in ways that can lead to harm.




This formulation assumes that all people have an inherent capacity for empathy. It doesn’t describe people as “lacking” empathy; that could imply that some people never had it, can’t attain it, or can’t recover it. Instead, the concept of “disrupted” empathy suggests an ability that can be regained.




Many different factors shape a person’s capacity for empathy, including past experiences, forms of neurodivergence, cultural norms, and more. This framework emphasizes the social dimensions of empathy, understanding it as a mode of relating that is modeled, given and received, learned and practiced over time. In this framing, we can conceive of empathy the way some linguists conceive of language: as an instinct inherent in our species but requiring social connection and learning to unlock and develop.




This conception draws on the abolitionist insight that both the structural and individual changes are necessary if we are to do away with harm. As we work with particular people to help restore their empathetic connection to others, we can also create social structures that reinforce empathy.













Empathy and Sexual Harm




Could this framework provide a more accurate assessment of the impact of sexual violence and similar forms of harm?




In some cases, experiencing sexual harm can disrupt a person’s capacity for empathy. This is most likely to result when the harm occurs in conjunction with other forms of physical and emotional abuse, especially if those are severe forms or take place at an early age. When a person starts out without safe and supportive relationships in which empathy can be modeled and received, that can inhibit the formation of such relationships later in life.




One of the most important components of healing from the trauma of such experiences involves receiving empathy—being believed and taken seriously, having one’s pain validated and grieved. This kind of recognition can form part of a healing journey that can restore disrupted empathy, significantly reducing the possibility that the healing person will harm others.




Often, experiencing sexual harm can 

intensify

 empathy. Many survivors become deeply attuned to the dynamics of consent and more conscientious about their interactions with others. Many become supporters and advocates themselves, transforming their experiences of hurt from liabilities into strengths as they offer empathy to other survivors.




This intensified empathy can feel like a double-edged sword. Sometimes it takes the form of heightened sensitivity to references to sexual assault, which can be dysregulating. It can also show up as becoming a particularly caring friend, a skilled counselor, a determined advocate, or a powerful organizer against violence.




The intensified empathy that can emerge out of experiences of trauma can become a super power, if sometimes an overwhelming one to possess. In touch with their emotions and acutely aware of the pain they experienced, many survivors are particularly attuned to others’ feelings and aware of the ways that they impact others. These qualities make them less likely to cause harm than the average person.




Survivors of sexual violence who fear that their experience may dispose them towards harming others should take heart. It is not the experience of being hurt but a condition of disrupted empathy that leads people to hurt others.




No one can undo what we’ve experienced in the past, but we can take proactive steps to restore empathy. We can actively work to address our own trauma, rebuild a sense of safety and connection, share our experiences with others, and keep listening and learning. In doing so, we can heal ourselves and ensure that the cycle of harm ends with us.













Disrupted Empathy, Oppression, and Entitlement




Experiencing hurt is not the only thing that can disrupt empathy. There are much more common root causes.




Let’s add another layer to our abolitionist analysis of harm:




Oppressive systems that engender entitlement

 

can also disrupt empathy.




Consider patriarchy, a system of oppression that is central to sexual violence. Patriarchy is a system of institutions and social relations that concentrate power for men at the expense of women and others. This system enables men to feel entitled to the labor, bodies, care, and obedience of women and others. Masculinity is defined in part by this sense of entitlement, while empathy is coded as feminine.




The masculine ideal of repressing emotions and remaining impervious to pain cuts off men’s empathy for themselves. This normalizes seeing others as weak and inferior if they feel pain themselves, or if they empathize with the pain of others. Gender norms train men, and all those who aspire to masculine power, into disrupted empathy.




Rape culture feeds on this disrupted empathy. Sexual violence could not exist without disregard for others’ pain and entitlement to others’ bodies. Oppressive gendered power structures bear far more responsibility than “hurt people hurting people” for the disrupted empathy that enables people to cause harm.




A great deal of evidence suggests that sexual violence flourishes in settings or social groups where collective norms support or excuse it. In other words, contexts in which sexual violence often occurs are not simply places that happen to include lots of pathological individuals. All people have a capacity to treat others with respect and consideration or with disregard and contempt. How people choose to treat others depends largely on the norms that predominate in those settings and groups.




It’s not surprising that the settings in which high rates of sexual violence have been documented—such as some fraternity houses, military units, and prisons—are male-dominated environments in which rituals that disrupt empathy are central to social norms. Hazing ceremonies, abusive officers or guards, and dehumanizing language and treatment all model relations devoid of empathy. In such environments, expressing feelings, showing care, and relating to others’ pain can indicate weakness, making someone a target for ridicule, exclusion, and violence. In these mostly single-sex environments where misogynist attitudes predominate, it’s not surprising that participants often direct sexual violence at women, trans and queer people, and others perceived as effeminate.




Another social structure that disrupts empathy is whiteness. Hundreds of years of racist violence and domination could not have taken place without white supremacy, an ideology that numbs its adherents to the pain of those whose humanity it denies. As 

Mab Segrest

 argues in 

Memoir of a Race Traitor

, a key component of white culture and identity established in the era of slavery and persisting to this day is 

anesthesia

, a deliberate repression of sensation and empathy towards racialized people. White supremacy is not just a belief about the superiority of one group defined as a race over another. It’s a claim about who is entitled to land, labor, resources, and bodies.




Sexual violence was central the antebellum economy, as enslavers utilized rape to reproduce the enslaved workforce and increase white intergenerational wealth. White men’s sense of entitlement to the bodies of people of color, particularly women and trans people, persists today in countless forms, from high rates of sexual violence and differential treatment of survivors of color in the criminal legal system to the racist tropes that saturate mainstream pornography.




So long as whiteness persists as a system for distributing power, its disruption of empathy will reinforce cycles of racial and gendered violence.




Yet there is no simple equation between identity and disrupted empathy. It is true that privilege—not having to think about the oppression that others experience—and a lack of shared experience frequently disrupt the empathy of those socialized as men and positioned as white. But there is nothing inherent in any demographic that produces disrupted empathy. Those from dominant groups can be deeply empathetic, and those from oppressed groups can experience disrupted empathy as well.




All people are capable of harming others, though patterns of social power distribute those harms unevenly. Developing an analysis of the origins of social harm in disrupted empathy can enable abolitionists to craft effective strategies for responding to it while dismantling the carceral structures that exacerbate its root causes.




While patriarchy and white supremacy form two of the oppressive systems most central to the entitlement and disrupted empathy that drive sexual violence, they are by no means the only ones. The “corrective” rape of lesbian women and the hate-fueled sexual assaults on gay men and trans people reflect the ongoing power of homophobia and transphobia. The persistence of inaccessible spaces throughout much of the American landscape reflects the entitlement many non-disabled people feel to convenience, low costs, or familiarity over disabled people’s ability to participate in public life. The horrific assaults that 

ICE

 and 

the Border Patrol

 are perpetrating against immigrant communities feed on narratives framing immigrants as dangerous outsiders undeserving of empathy.




These oppressive structures—and many others like them—interrupt the basic intuitive feelings of connection and concern we feel towards other people, rendering it possible to concentrate power through artificial social divisions. These structures, far more than individual experiences of hurt, are the root cause of persistent sexual violence and other patterns of harm in our society.













Opposing Empathy to Reinforce Hierarchy




Empathy disrupts oppression; disrupted empathy reinforces oppression. In view of this, it is not surprising that many of the wealthiest and most privileged people in our society today are trying to 

discredit empathy itself

. They want to convince us that selfishness and disregard for others’ suffering—the qualities that have enabled them to amass wealth and power at our expense—are natural and healthy, while connection and solidarity are pernicious.




Elon Musk is leading this charge. In an appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast, the world’s first trillionaire 

claimed

, “The fundamental weakness of Western civilization is empathy.” His rant combined racist anxiety about immigration and changing demographics in “the West” with gendered fears over women’s autonomy and trans people’s existence. As a successful capitalist, it is not surprising that he is promoting competition and economic inequality as desirable for their own sake.




But Elon Musk is not alone. Figures from the Christian Right speak of “

the sin of empathy

,” reframing what is usually seen as a virtue as harmful and citing tolerance for trans people as an example of its “destructive” consequences. Religious critics accuse progressives of deploying “

toxic empathy

” to undermine Biblical morality, citing those who defend reproductive autonomy because they care about pregnant women at least as much as their unborn fetuses. Conservative academics warn that “

suicidal empathy

” subverts logical thought and optimal decision-making, allegedly undermining “Western” society by causing people to accept poor/non-white/Muslim immigration.




Why do MAGA and the far right feel so threatened by empathy today?




Perhaps because their entire program of hierarchy and domination would be undermined if people were fully able to feel and act on the misery that it inflicts on the vast majority of the global population. Perhaps because nationalism, racism, patriarchy, and transphobia could not survive if people from dominant groups considered perspectives and feelings beyond their own. Perhaps because modes of relating based in empathy—such as solidarity and mutual aid—point to the possibility of a way of life beyond capitalism and the state.




Empathy alone won’t suffice to tear down the systems of oppression that confine us, but it’s an essential first step. It connects our responses to interpersonal harm on an individual level to our organizing to transform society on a collective level. It is the keystone of an abolitionist future. That is why it is intolerable to those invested in propping up the ruling order today.













Conclusion: Empathy and Abolition




Abolition requires restoring disrupted empathy. This must go in both directions: it means restoring the empathy that those who have caused harm feel towards those they harmed, while also 

insisting on empathy for people who have caused harm

 as essential to the process of transformation.




By contrast, the core principle of the criminal legal system is the negation of empathy. No one could administer punishments ranging from fines to caging to execution without cutting themselves off from empathy for those they punish. The state’s entire concept of “justice” revolves around perpetually inflicting harm and suppressing empathy. Is it any wonder that our society continues to suffer from forms of behavior stemming from disrupted empathy when one of the chief forces actively disrupting our empathy is the “justice” system itself?




This doesn’t mean that if we simply treated people better and listened to their feelings, no one would hurt anyone. Disrupted empathy isn’t the only cause of harmful behavior, but it is an enabling condition for it. As such, it is a root cause that abolitionists can work to address. And since the primary “solutions” that our criminal legal system offers are explicitly premised on rejecting empathy, this framework offers us a clear basis for rejecting carceral responses.




Let’s let go of the narrative that “hurt people hurt people.” At best, it serves to humanize people who hurt others and to call for responses that interrupt cycles of harm. But it also reinforces hurtful myths, redirects attention from structural to individual factors, and misdiagnoses the root causes of harm.




Instead, let’s tell a broader story about the foundations of social harm that suggests concrete steps we can take to redress it. Focusing on disrupted empathy rather than past experiences of hurt offers a more holistic and accurate account of sexual violence in particular and interpersonal harm in general.




Abolition means more than simply doing away with prisons and police. It requires us to reconnect to our basic capacity to see and feel one another’s humanity. To restore our collective empathy as a culture, we must dismantle the structures of social oppression that have disrupted it.




Those who have been hurt by rape culture, patriarchy, white supremacy, and other harmful systems have a vital role to play in this ongoing struggle. Not because they, as hurt people, are especially likely to hurt others—they aren’t—but because the insights that their experiences offer can equip them to step out of the endless cycles of harm perpetuated by carceral systems and craft a renewed vision of liberation anchored in empathy for all.
















Images courtesy of Frans Masereel. As he put it, “An ideal communism would be, let us say, an anarchic sort of communism.”

title: Giorgio Agamben: The death of the word?
content:
Michelangelo, 

Cumaean Sibyl

 (c. 1511), Sistine Chapel, Vatican City




This short article was originally published under the title “Morte della parola?” in the Italian newspaper 

Paese Sera

 on 8 February 1968. It has been republished in the latest issue of the French magazine 

Entétement

, although the original version can be found on the 

La Voce di Fiore

 archive website. A Spanish translation of the same can be found at th magazine 

Ficción de la razón

.







A book has recently been published in Paris, 

Of Grammatology

 (1967), a work destined to cause a stir not only in the field of linguistic studies. Jacques Derrida, one of the most original figures in the new wave of French philosophical criticism, begins with the observation that, today, “through a movement whose necessity we can barely glimpse, everything that, for at least twenty centuries, has tended to be defined under the name of language, is beginning to be summarised under the name of writing”. It does indeed seem that writing—which, according to Rousseau, was nothing more than a complement to speech—is gradually freeing itself from its subordination to the phonetic medium, to the point of reversing its traditional relationship with language: writing would therefore not be a technique in the service of language, but rather, on the contrary, it is language that can be considered a specific case, an aspect, of writing.







To better understand the phenomenon to which Derrida refers when he speaks of writing dissociated from the phonetic element, one need only consider the example of mathematics, whose symbolic notation does not refer to any spoken language. If we consider that today we are witnessing a process of mathematisation across all the sciences, the “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon (readers who have followed recent news regarding the 

in vitro

 synthesis of living matter, carried out by certain American scientists, will recall having heard talk of writing and “programmes” even in relation to the most elementary processes of the living cell). The “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon.




On the basis of these premises, Derrida deduces the need for a pure science of writing, which considers writing prior to speech and independently of it: this science is, precisely, “grammatology”; and, to define its aims, it suffices to substitute this term for “semiology”, the term Saussure uses to outline the programme of his famous 

Course in General Linguistics

: “We shall call it grammatology… and, as it does not yet exist, we cannot say what it will be; but it has a right to exist, and its place is determined in advance”. The age of speech, which began under the creative power of the verb, is drawing to a close before our very eyes; the character of this new age might be summed up in the following formula: “In the beginning was the written word’’.




Whilst it is true that, from this perspective, linguistics must become a mere branch of grammatology, Derrida seems, however, to overlook the fact that a science already exists which considers language not as speech, but as code and writing; consequently, grammatology itself should necessarily be understood as a sub-branch or a section of that science. This is cybernetics, which, from its beginnings in Wiener’s theories, defined its world as a universe of writing and coding. The very idea of grammatology is already fully contained within the notion of “programme”, one of the key concepts of cybernetics. Etymologically, “programme” —pro-grammer— means “to put the letter (that is, 

writing

) first”, whilst “prophecy” means, by contrast, “to put the word first”. Indeed, in the programme assigned to an electronic brain, everything that constitutes the living, phonetic element of language is erased to make way for a system of absolute writing that can be deciphered but not pronounced. It is fair to say that, up to now, our civilisation has known two types of language that have gradually diverged: the language of science is, essentially, written language —code, writing—, whilst the language of poetry and philosophical thought is spoken language —breath, word—. Nevertheless, these two domains—which, for convenience’s sake, we might call the “sphere of the programme” and the “sphere of prophecy”—are drawing ever closer together today thanks to cybernetics; through the mathematisation of human phenomena, cybernetics tends to erase any distinction between the natural sciences and the human sciences, between programme and prophecy. With cybernetics and information theory, our relationship with language is changing without us being fully aware of it. The time of things that can be said is over: the time of things that can only be written down, encoded, is beginning. In the beginning was the written word… Does technology not present us daily with products whose names seem to be mere words, but which, in reality, can only be written and encoded using acronyms? The reduction of linguistics to “grammatology” is but one aspect of this process.




Once this has come to an end, the entire realm of language will become the realm of the unspeakable, even though, on the surface, we shall continue to speak. Faced with this eclipse of the word, rather than seeking from now on the foundations of a possible science of writing, should we not instead reflect deeply on the reasons for this obscuration, so that the word may once again become what it is: not merely the code for information, but the reality that underpins and gives meaning to our existence on earth?

title: Our founder: Charlotte Wilson
content:
Charlotte Wilson at Newnham College, Cambridge, c.1873







From our 140th anniversary issue, an appreciation of the unfairly obscured anarchist and her profound legacy




punkacademic, from 

Freedom News

, 15/11/2026




“The key-note of the anarchist contention is that the vitiation of social life is produced by the domination of man by man. The spirit of domination is the disintegrating element, which, constantly tending to break up society, is the fundamental cause of confusion and disorder.” So wrote Charlotte Wilson in July 1886 – a few months before she and a group of others founded the Freedom newspaper and in turn Freedom Press.







Aside from the gendered language, Wilson’s analysis still has relevance today, as does her writing. Her emphasis on the role of domination in disrupting the social relations to which she felt human beings naturally inclined would find its echoes in more recent times.




In 1982, Murray Bookchin spoke of domination as the fundamental vice to which his social ecology stood opposed. “The domination of nature by man”, wrote Bookchin, in his 

Ecology of Freedom

, “stems from the very real domination of human by human”. Bookchin paid tribute to a litany of male writers – Weber, Horkheimer, Adorno, Polanyi, and Kropotkin. He also named his “favourite Utopian” – Wilson’s former friend and comrade, William Morris. But of Wilson, mention came there none.




Bookchin’s assertion that before the 1960s “domination” and “hierarchy” would have been unfamiliar terms on the left would have seemed strange to Wilson. Despite the best efforts of scholars such as Susan Hinely, Hermia Oliver and our own Nicolas Walter in the decades since Bookchin, Wilson remains unfairly obscured. And yet her legacy – not least the enduring one of this periodical itself – was profound.




Born in 1854 in Worcestershire, Charlotte “Lettie” Martin (as she was before marriage) was solidly middle-class, born into an era of religious upheaval, scientific discovery, and political and economic change.




It was a period of huge extremes of wealth and poverty; Dickens’s 

Hard Times

 was published the same year Lettie was born, its soulless Mr Gradgrind as the epitome of drudgery and conformity. Lettie – our Charlotte Wilson – would not do conformity.




Hinely notes that Wilson’s heritage was evangelical, and that religious sentiment pervaded her upbringing even as she repudiated the church in favour of her secular faiths – socialism in general, and anarchism in particular. But religious language and a sense of mission characterises her writing.




She was from her youth a rebel. Her gender meant she could not vote nor receive a degree in the ancient universities where her male peers might venture. She went anyway – to Cambridge, as one of the first women to attend classes there. Married in 1876 to Arthur Wilson, a stockbroker, she lived in London and cultivated a wide intellectual circle on the left. Cambridge had been a transformative experience for her and, as Hinely shows, gave her an understanding of social science which accelerated her transition to socialist politics.




She was radicalised by a series of incidents in the 1880s. The Lyon Trial of the 66—which amounted to a purge of anarchists by the French governmen—saw the famous writer Peter Kropotkin and many others jailed for purported membership of the Black International, and was widely discussed in the press. Wilson spoke French, often travelled to France, and read Kropotkin and Elisee Reclus as she was taking her steps into the fluid socialist circles of London in the 1880s.




By 1885, she was a self-declared anarchist and penning articles for periodicals under the pseudonym ‘An English Anarchist’. By early 1886 she was in touch with Sophie Kropotkin, Peter’s wife, and following his release encouraged the family to move to London where the Kropotkins settled for the next several decades in exile.




She had resolved to found a new anarchist paper, focused on propaganda for anarchist socialism—Wilson was herself an anarchist communist—and with Kropotkin on board she took up the reins as the paper’s first editor. There is not space here to do justice to all her achievements, but she edited the paper for most of the next decade.




Her most substantive legacy is the establishment and survival of 

Freedom

 at a time when other anarchist journals foundered. But she was more than that. Wilson has been a victim of “manarchism” as Ruth Kinna has called it, or the tendency for men in the movement to reduce the contributions of women. In Wilson’s comments on domination, we can see the scope of her thought on anarchism and its applicability to our own struggles today.




She wrote on work, the family, propaganda of the deed, the philosophy and morality of anarchism, and much besides. Her writing and thought repay overdue attention. She was no sectarian, as Hinely and Oliver note, and sought to bring diverse currents in the movement together whilst maintaining her own clear stance, as her paper has done in the 140 years since.




As she said then, so we say now: “We are socialists, disbelievers in property… we are anarchists, disbelievers in government … in any shape and under any pretext.”

Freedom

 anarchist journal, issue 86:2







A General View

 (1888)




Charlotte Wilson




When we cast a broad glance upon the history of mankind, we see one distinctive feature pervading it from the remotest antiquity up to our own times. On the one aide there are the masses toiling, laboring creating wealth by the labor of their hands, and asking for nothing else -but peace, liberty, and equality among themselves. And on the other side there is a minority, sometimes of foreign conquerors, and sometimes natives of the country itself, who continually aim dominating the masses, at freely enjoying the fruits of their labor, and at rendering their own rule everlasting by means of Law and Force, by an appropriate education, and religious teachings. All the history of mankind is nothing but that struggle between the two hostile forces.




The pretext under which the rule of the minority is imposed upon the masses may vary to some extent in the course of centuries ; but in fact it remains always the same, whatever the minor differences it ,assumes. Those who pretend to rule over the people maintain that the people are unable to protect themselves against foreign aggressors; that they are unable to keep internal peace ; unable to organize themselves so as to permit to everybody the free exercise of his faculties; and that they-the minority of would-be rulers-are able to secure all this. If they restrain the liberty of the individual, it is only to give the fullest amount of liberty to society. And always through history, from its very dawn until now, we see that the minority of rulers do not keep their promise. They promise peace, and they bring war, external and internal. They promise liberty, and they bring oppression. They promise wealth and harmony, and they bring misery and disorder.




In olden times the baron arms gangs of soldiers-of robbers-in order to protect the laborer„from other gangs of robbers. “Till the ground in peace, we shall be on the watch,” he says. But soon his gangs begin to oppress the laborers worse than the supposed foreign enemy. They plunder the peasant’s house; they quarrel with one another. The peasant toils; he exhausts himself in labor to maintain the baron, his guests, and his soldiers-but be has no peace. His fields and his home are continually devastated; but he must put up with that rule, because he has no arms, and they ‘are armed ; fie has no knowledge of warfare, and they have made warfare their specialty. He bears that oppression until finally he revolts-and we witness all over Europe the peasants’ wars..




Later on, the king becomes his ruler. One of those robber-barons succeeds in overpowering the others, with the support of the masses. He promises to the peasant that he will prevent the barons from ruining the tiller of the soil by their continuous wars and exactions. Instead of the arbitrary and vexatious taxation by the barons the king introduces a kind of uniform taxation for the benefit of the Crown, which enables, him to levy and to drill an army, and to crush the rebel barons. He solemnly promises never to levy any taxes but those agreed upon by the Commons themselves. He grants full liberty to the cities, and within their walls we see wealth grow, trades develop, arts flourish. Supported by the towns and villages, the king succeeds in crushing the robber-barons who infest the country,„partly by force, but chiefly by money paid out of the pockets of the peasantry ; and soon he becomes the supreme ruler of the country.




Does a time of prosperity soon follow? No; because the peasant and the city artisan soon feel the pressure of the new power. The king has never enough taxes, and he intrigues, be creates parties to bring the council of the Commons under his personal authority. Having an army at his disposal, he involves the country in wars, and the taxes steadily grow. Be nominates officials, who are as vexatious as the barons of old. By and by he interferes with the internal affairs of the cities, creates parties within their walls, and under the pretext of protecting the poor against the rich, he breaks down their independence. After a few centuries of monarchy, peasant and citizen perceive that they are slaves again : slaves of the king and his court. Poverty and misery grow,„and a new revolt breaks out.




But revolt is already more difficult. The revolted peasants and artisans have to fight against a big army. They are opposed by thousands of men who have private interests that have grown up under the monarchy; they have to combat thousands of privileges, and also thousands of prejudices. To crush those forces they are bound to ally themselves with the growing middle classes against the court ; and they have also to reckon with newly-developed prejudices, The king has not established his rule by brute force alone. Thousands of lawyers, priests, and teachers have been busied for whole centuries in spreading ideas of submission to the royal authority, and bestowing on it the sanction of both science and divinity. Thousands of prejudices as to the benefits of that central authority have been nurtured by appropriate teachings and literature. And the revolution must be made in men’s minds, as well as in the palace. Therefore, instead of making a revolution to liberate the masses, instead of reverting to the principles of freedom and decentralized organization, a new central authority is created in the parliament,




The parliament begins with the fairest promises. Again, there will be no taxes but those freely agreed to by the nation. Like the king in the first days of monarchy, the middle-class representatives begin by promising peace, security of life, freedom. They will listen to the voice of the nation, and never legislate otherwise than in accordance with that voice. The interests of the laborer and workman will be their supreme rule. 11 Only obey the parliament better than you have obeyed the king, and all will be right.” They have seen that force alone will not do, and they try to establish their reign on persuasion. They surround parliament with a kind of sacredness; by their books, their schools, their press. they try to convince the nation of the benefits of parliamentary rule. University and pulpit unite in supporting parliament. The political powers are more and more concentrated, and the political machinery becomes so intricate as to make people believe that only men of superior intelligence, guided by a Peel, a Palmerstone, a Beaconsfield, or a Gladstone, are capable of holding the rudder of the nation amid ” the tempests.” All must be centralized in the hands of these saviors of the people.




But there comes a time when the masses begin to perceive that they have been cheated once again. The promised peace does not come; wars, and Loans to pay their expenses, become a chronic disease. The parliament becomes a nest of intrigues. It does nothing, it can do nothing. The slightest reform, like the repeal of corn laws or Home Rule for Ireland, can be obtained only by open revolt. The rule of the middle classes has resulted in oppression as bad as that of the barons of old. Industry is ruined, agriculture is ruined, foreign trade is ruined; terrible industrial and commercial crises succeed one another, and there is no better outlook for the future, And while the rulers do their utmost to maintain their rule and enforce the ideas of respect for authority, the masses lose that respect, and perceive that the rule of the middle classes and parliamentary rule altogether cannot last. New schemes are discussed; the necessity of a new departure becomes universally felt.




But what will be that new departure? Will it be a fresh remodeling of the institutions of private property, centralized government, and representation? Will it be again a repetition of the errors committed when absolute monarchy was substituted for the rule of the barons, or the parliament for absolute monarchy I Or must it be really a new departure?




The time has come for a really new departure. It becomes generally understood among the workers that the real basis of all human organization must be the equality of its members and their liberty to organize themselves according to their own needs. It becomes evident that political liberty is possible only where there is economical equality-; that the laborer who tills the ground for the landlord never will be the political equal of the landlord, nor the factory worker the equal of his employer, nor the ruled the equal of the ruler.




It becomes evident that all the wealth which we see around us has not been created by those who now possess it, but has been appropriated by them owing to a vicious social organization, And it becomes obvious that as long as all the affairs of the nation –education, industry, commerce, navigation, national defense-are left in the hands of a central government, there can be nothing but what we see now, a state of affairs which has become unbearable for the masses.




A new departure must be made in a new direction. Monarchy has centralized all the life of the nation in its hands, and parliament has merely continued what monarchy has begun. We must decentralize. Thousands of cities and villages have their own interests, and they are the best judges of those interests. As to the nation, it can be nothing but the free union of those independent units. The twenty-two independent republics of Switzerland (the centralizers call them cantons) are as well united together ; they are as much one nation„even more of a nation-than the centralized monarchies and republics. And yet they are as independent as each of those monarchies. They only make contracts for the achievement of certain common aims. But the Swiss republics are not united within themselves, because each of them has repeated on a smaller scale the errors of the big centralized kingdoms, and therefore we see within them also the growing tendency towards a return to the time when each commune was as independent as each of the little republics (cantons) is now , when the republicitself was but a federation of free communes.




But even supposing these political changes, unity within each commune will not exist as long as there are within that commune the rich possessor of wealth and the hired laborer. And therefore the next step must be-and will be-the common possession by the whole of the commune of all its wealth : houses and gardens, fields and streets, manufactories and railways.




Already now we may see municipalities in possession of beautiful public buildings, universities, theaters, gardens, libraries, gas-works, tramways, railways, grain elevators, farms, docks, and so on. For, being managed by the city instead of private individuals, they are none the worse. But all this wealth„theaters and universities, beautiful streets and gardens„remains for the use of the few ; the bare-footed boy who falls into an exhausted sleep with a bundle of newspapers under his arm on the steps of a theater has no possibility of sharing in the enjoyment of that theater, or of the intellectual pleasures of the university. The street and its brilliant illumination are no joy for him. He is an outcast of society. And yet he is as well entitled to enjoy all that as the millionaire’s son. And therefore the next step to be taken is that the city must add to its parks and theaters, to its schools and tramways, the manufactory and the dwelling house.




It must take possession of these, and, by organizing labor on the, principles of equality, it will abolish the distinction between the sons of the ex-outcast and the ex-millionaire. Both will work in the same workshop ; both will cultivate the same garden, run the same tramway. They will be equal economically and politically. And then they will be free.




The nation of the future will be the federation of these free organisms, economically and politically free. Slaves cannot easily federate ; free men can and do. Arid free communes, freely federated, will constitute a nation much more closely united than the nations which consist now of Rothschilds and paupers.




But, however limited its area, the commune must not repeat within itself the error of entrusting a few men with the management of all its affairs; it must not commit the error of creating municipal parliaments which will be as instrumental for the creation of privileges as the national parliament has been. It must organize itself on the principle of “no rulers.”

title: Remembering “remembrance day” with Randolph Bourne
content:
It cannot be too firmly realized that war is a function of States and not of nations, indeed that it is the chief function of States. War is a very artificial thing. It is not the naive spontaneous outburst of herd pugnacity; it is no more primary than is formal religion. War cannot exist without a military establishment, and a military establishment cannot exist without a State organization. War has an immemorial tradition and heredity only because the State has a long tradition and heredity. But they are inseparably and functionally joined. We cannot crusade against war without crusading implicitly against the State. And we cannot expect, or take measures to ensure, that this war is a war to end war, unless at the same time we take measures to end the State in its traditional form. The State is not the nation, and the State can be modified and even abolished in its present form, without harming the nation. On the contrary, with the passing of the dominance of the State, the genuine life-enhancing forces of the nation will be liberated. If the State’s chief function is war, then the State must suck out of the nation a large part of its energy for purely sterile purposes of defense and aggression. It devotes to waste or to actual destruction as much as it can of the vitality of the nation. No one will deny that war is a vast complex of life-destroying and life-crippling forces. If the State’s chief function is war, then it is chiefly concerned with coordinating and developing the powers and techniques which make for destruction. And this means not only the actual and potential destruction of the enemy, but of the nation at home as well. For the very existence of a State in a system of States means that the nation lies always under a risk of war and invasion, and the calling away of energy into military pursuits means a crippling of the productive and life-enhancing process of the national life.







The State

 (1919)




Randolph Bourne




from 

The Anarchist Library

: “Randolph Bourne left an unfinished, unpaginated draft of 

The State

 when he died during the flu pandemic of 1918. The draft was published posthumously, with some material incorrectly ordered, in 

Untimely Papers

 (1919). This edition follows the corrected ordering used in most printed editions of Bourne’s work.”







I.




To most Americans of the classes which consider themselves significant the war brought a sense of the sanctity of the State which, if they had had time to think about it, would have seemed a sudden and surprising alteration in their habits of thought. In times of peace, we usually ignore the State in favour of partisan political controversies, or personal struggles for office, or the pursuit of party policies. It is the Government rather than the State with which the politically minded are concerned. The State is reduced to a shadowy emblem which comes to consciousness only on occasions of patriotic holiday.







Government is obviously composed of common and unsanctified men, and is thus a legitimate object of criticism and even contempt. If your own party is in power, things may be assumed to be moving safely enough; but if the opposition is in, then clearly all safety and honor have fled the State. Yet you do not put it to yourself in quite that way. What you think is only that there are rascals to be turned out of a very practical machinery of offices and functions which you take for granted. When we say that Americans are lawless, we usually mean that they are less conscious than other peoples of the august majesty of the institution of the State as it stands behind the objective government of men and laws which we see. In a republic the men who hold office are indistinguishable from the mass. Very few of them possess the slightest personal dignity with which they could endow their political role; even if they ever thought of such a thing. And they have no class distinction to give them glamour. In a republic the Government is obeyed grumblingly, because it has no bedazzlements or sanctities to gild it. If you are a good old-fashioned democrat, you rejoice at this fact, you glory in the plainness of a system where every citizen has become a king. If you are more sophisticated you bemoan the passing of dignity and honor from affairs of State. But in practice, the democrat does not in the least treat his elected citizen with the respect due to a king, nor does the sophisticated citizen pay tribute to the dignity even when he finds it. The republican State has almost no trappings to appeal to the common man’s emotions. What it has are of military origin, and in an unmilitary era such as we have passed through since the Civil War, even military trappings have been scarcely seen. In such an era the sense of the State almost fades out of the consciousness of men.




With the shock of war, however, the State comes into its own again. The Government, with no mandate from the people, without consultation of the people, conducts all the negotiations, the backing and filling, the menaces and explanations, which slowly bring it into collision with some other Government, and gently and irresistibly slides the country into war. For the benefit of proud and haughty citizens, it is fortified with a list of the intolerable insults which have been hurled toward us by the other nations; for the benefit of the liberal and beneficent, it has a convincing set of moral purposes which our going to war will achieve; for the ambitious and aggressive classes, it can gently whisper of a bigger role in the destiny of the world. The result is that, even in those countries where the business of declaring war is theoretically in the hands of representatives of the people, no legislature has ever been known to decline the request of an Executive, which has conducted all foreign affairs in utter privacy and irresponsibility, that it order the nation into battle. Good democrats are wont to feel the crucial difference between a State in which the popular Parliament or Congress declares war, and the State in which an absolute monarch or ruling class declares war. But, put to the stern pragmatic test, the difference is not striking. In the freest of republics as well as in the most tyrannical of empires, all foreign policy, the diplomatic negotiations which produce or forestall war, are equally the private property of the Executive part of the Government, and are equally exposed to no check whatever from popular bodies, or the people voting as a mass themselves.




The moment war is declared, however, the mass of the people, through some spiritual alchemy, become convinced that they have willed and executed the deed themselves. They then, with the exception of a few malcontents, proceed to allow themselves to be regimented, coerced, deranged in all the environments of their lives, and turned into a solid manufactory of destruction toward whatever other people may have, in the appointed scheme of things, come within the range of the Government’s disapprobation. The citizen throws off his contempt and indifference to Government, identifies himself with its purposes, revives all his military memories and symbols, and the State once more walks, an august presence, through the imaginations of men. Patriotism becomes the dominant feeling, and produces immediately that intense and hopeless confusion between the relations which the individual bears and should bear toward the society of which he is a part.




The patriot loses all sense of the distinction between State, nation, and government. In our quieter moments, the Nation or Country forms the basic idea of society. We think vaguely of a loose population spreading over a certain geographical portion of the earth’s surface, speaking a common language, and living in a homogeneous civilization. Our idea of Country concerns itself with the non-political aspects of a people, its ways of living, its personal traits, its literature and art, its characteristic attitudes toward life. We are Americans because we live in a certain bounded territory, because our ancestors have carried on a great enterprise of pioneering and colonization, because we live in certain kinds of communities which have a certain look and express their aspirations in certain ways. We can see that our civilization is different from contiguous civilizations like the Indian and Mexican. The institutions of our country form a certain network which affects us vitally and intrigues our thoughts in a way that these other civilizations do not. We are a part of Country, for better or for worse. We have arrived in it through the operation of physiological laws, and not in any way through our own choice. By the time we have reached what are called years of discretion, its influences have molded our habits, our values, our ways of thinking, so that however aware we may become, we never really lose the stamp of our civilization, or could be mistaken for the child of any other country. Our feeling for our fellow countrymen is one of similarity or of mere acquaintance. We may be intensely proud of and congenial to our particular network of civilization, or we may detest most of its qualities and rage at its defects. This does not alter the fact that we are inextricably bound up in it. The Country, as an inescapable group into which we are born, and which makes us its particular kind of a citizen of the world, seems to be a fundamental fact of our consciousness, an irreducible minimum of social feeling.




Now this feeling for country is essentially noncompetitive; we think of our own people merely as living on the earth’s surface along with other groups, pleasant or objectionable as they may be, but fundamentally as sharing the earth with them. In our simple conception of country there is no more feeling of rivalry with other peoples than there is in our feeling for our family. Our interest turns within rather than without, is intensive and not belligerent. We grow up and our imaginations gradually stake out the world we live in, they need no greater conscious satisfaction for their gregarious impulses than this sense of a great mass of people to whom we are more or less attuned, and in whose institutions we are functioning. The feeling for country would be an uninflatable maximum were it not for the ideas of State and Government which are associated with it. Country is a concept of peace, of tolerance, of living and letting live. But State is essentially a concept of power, of competition: it signifies a group in its aggressive aspects. And we have the misfortune of being born not only into a country but into a State, and as we grow up we learn to mingle the two feelings into a hopeless confusion.




The State is the country acting as a political unit, it is the group acting as a repository of force, determiner of law, arbiter of justice. International politics is a “power politics” because it is a relation of States and that is what States infallibly and calamitously are, huge aggregations of human and industrial force that may be hurled against each other in war. When a country acts as a whole in relation to another country, or in imposing laws on its own inhabitants, or in coercing or punishing individuals or minorities, it is acting as a State. The history of America as a country is quite different from that of America as a State. In one case it is the drama of the pioneering conquest of the land, of the growth of wealth and the ways in which it was used, of the enterprise of education, and the carrying out of spiritual ideals, of the struggle of economic classes. But as a State, its history is that of playing a part in the world, making war, obstructing international trade, preventing itself from being split to pieces, punishing those citizens whom society agrees are offensive, and collecting money to pay for all.




Government on the other hand is synonymous with neither State nor Nation. It is the machinery by which the nation, organized as a State, carries out its State functions. Government is a framework of the administration of laws, and the carrying out of the public force. Government is the idea of the State put into practical operation in the hands of definite, concrete, fallible men. It is the visible sign of the invisible grace. It is the word made flesh. And it has necessarily the limitations inherent in all practicality. Government is the only form in which we can envisage the State, but it is by no means identical with it. That the State is a mystical conception is something that must never be forgotten. Its glamor and its significance linger behind the framework of Government and direct its activities.




Wartime brings the ideal of the State out into very clear relief, and reveals attitudes and tendencies that were hidden. In times of peace the sense of the State flags in a republic that is not militarized. For war is essentially the health of the State. The ideal of the State is that within its territory its power and influence should be universal. As the Church is the medium for the spiritual salvation of man, so the State is thought of as the medium for his political salvation. Its idealism is a rich blood flowing to all the members of the body politic. And it is precisely in war that the urgency for union seems greatest, and the necessity for universality seems most unquestioned. The State is the organization of the herd to act offensively or defensively against another herd similarly organized. The more terrifying the occasion for defense, the closer will become the organization and the more coercive the influence upon each member of the herd. War sends the current of purpose and activity flowing down to the lowest levels of the herd, and to its remote branches. All the activities of society are linked together as fast as possible to this central purpose of making a military offensive or military defense, and the State becomes what in peacetimes it has vainly struggled to become — the inexorable arbiter and determinant of men’s businesses and attitudes and opinions. The slack is taken up, the cross-currents fade out, and the nation moves lumberingly and slowly, but with ever accelerated speed and integration, towards the great end, towards that “peacefulness of being at war,” of which L. P. Jacks has spoken so unforgettably.




The classes which are able to play an active and not merely a passive role in the organization for war get a tremendous liberation of activity and energy. Individuals are jolted out of their old routine, many of them are given new positions of responsibility, new techniques must be learnt. Wearing home times are broken and women who would have remained attached with infantile bonds are liberated for service overseas. A vast sense of rejuvenescence pervades the significant classes, a sense of new importance in the world. Old national ideals are taken out, re-adapted to the purpose and used as the universal touchstones, or molds into which all thought is poured. Every individual citizen who in peacetimes had no living fragment of hte State becomes an active amateur agent of the Government in reporting spies and disloyalists, in raising Government funds, or in propagating such measures as are considered necessary by officialdom. Minority opinion, which in times of peace was only irritating and could not be dealt with by law unless it was conjoined with actual crime, becomes with the outbreak of war, a case for outlawry. Criticism of the State, objections to war, lukewarm opinions concerning the necessity or the beauty of conscription, are made subject to ferocious penalties, far exceeding [in] severity those affixed to actual pragmatic crimes. Public opinion, as expressed in the newspapers, and the pulpits and the schools, becomes one solid block. “Loyalty,” or rather war orthodoxy, becomes the sole test for all professions, techniques, occupations. Particularly is this true in the sphere of the intellectual life. There the smallest taint is held to spread over the whole soul, so that a professor of physics is ipso facto disqualified to teach physics or hold honorable place in a university — the republic of learning — if he is at all unsound on the war. Even mere association with persons thus tainted is considered to disqualify a teacher. Anything pertaining to the enemy becomes taboo. His books are suppressed wherever possible, his language is forbidden. His artistic products are considered to convey in the subtlest spiritual way taints of vast poison to the soul that permits itself to enjoy them. So enemy music is suppressed, and energetic measures of opprobrium taken against those whose artistic consciences are not ready to perform such an act of self-sacrifice. The rage for loyal conformity works impartially, and often in diametric opposition to other orthodoxies and traditional conformities or ideals. The triumphant orthodoxy of the State is shown at its apex perhaps when Christian preachers lose their pulpits for taking in more or less literal terms the Sermon on the Mount, and Christian zealots are sent to prison for twenty years for distributing tracts which argue that war is unscriptural.




War is the health of the State. It automatically sets in motion throughout society those irresistible forces for uniformity, for passionate cooperation with the Government in coercing into obedience the minority groups and individuals which lack the larger herd sense. The machinery of government sets and enforces the drastic penalties. The minorities are either intimidated into silence, or brought slowly around by subtle process of persuasion which may seem to them really to be converting them. Of course, the ideal of perfect loyalty, perfect uniformity is never really attained. The classes upon whom the amateur work of coercion falls are unwearied in their zeal, but often their agitation, instead of converting merely serves to stiffen their resistance. Minorities are rendered sullen, and some intellectual opinion bitter and satirical. But in general, the nation in wartime attains a uniformity of feeling, a hierarchy of values culminating at the undisputed apex of the State ideal, which could not possibly be produced through any other agency than war. Other values such as artistic creation, knowledge, reason, beauty, the enhancement of life, are instantly and almost unanimously sacrificed, and the significant classes who have constituted themselves the amateur agents of the State, are engaged not only in sacrificing these values for themselves but in coercing all other persons into sacrificing them.




War — or at least modern war waged by a democratic republic against a powerful enemy — seems to achieve for a nation almost all that the most inflamed political idealist could desire. Citizens are no longer indifferent to their Government, but each cell of the body politic is brimming with life and activity. We are at last on the way to full realization of that collective community in which each individual somehow contains the virtue of the whole. In a nation at war, every citizen identifies himself with the whole and feels immensely strengthened in that identification. The purpose and desire of the collective community live in each person who throws himself whole-heartedly into the cause of war. The impeding distinction between society and the individual is almost blotted out. At war, the individual becomes almost identical with his society. He achieves a superb self-assurance, an intuition of the rightness of all his ideas and emotions, so that in the suppression of opponents or heretics he is invincibly strong; he feels behind him all the power of the collective community. The individual as social being in war seems to have achieved almost his apotheosis. Not for any religious impulse could the American nation have been expected to show such devotion 

en masse

, such sacrifice and labor. Certainly not for any secular good, such as universal education or the subjugation of nature, would it have poured forth its treasure and its life, or would it have permitted such stern coercive measures to be taken against it, such as conscripting its money and its men. But for the sake of a war of offensive self-defense, undertaken to support a difficult cause to the slogan of “democracy,” it would reach the highest level ever known of collective effort.




For these secular goods, connected with the enhancement of life, the education of men and the use of the intelligence to realize reason and beauty in the nation’s communal living, are alien to our traditional ideal of the State. The State is intimately connected with war, for it is the organization of the collective community when it acts in a political manner, and to act in a political manner towards a rival group has meant, throughout all history — war.




There is nothing invidious in the use of the term, “herd,” in connection with the State. It is merely an attempt to reduce closer to first principles the nature of this institution in the shadow of which we all live, move and have our being.
