They could be composed of the leaders of the propertied classes themselves or their lieutenants, who could retain their power indefinitely, or at least until they were unseated by rivals within the same charmed domain. They were at least entirely safe from attack by the officially constituted electorate, who, as the party system became mor and more firmly established, found they could vote only on slates set up for them by unknown councils behind an imposing and all-powerful “Party.”




As soon as this system was organized into a hierarchy extending from national down to state and county politics, it became perfectly safe to broaden the electorate. The clamors of the unpropertied or the less propertied to share in the selection of their democratic republican government could be graciously acceded to without endangering in the least the supremacy of those classes which the founders had meant to be supreme. The minority were now even more effectually protected from the majority than under the old system, however indirect the election might be. The electorate was now reduced to a ratifier of slates, both of which were pledged to upper-class domination; the electorate could have the freest, most universal suffrage, for any mass-desire for political change, any determined will to shift the class balance, would be obliged to register itself through the party machinery. It could make no frontal attack on the Government. And the party machinery was directly devised to absorb and neutralize this popular shock, handing out to the disgruntled electorate a disguised stone when it asked for political bread, and effectually smashing any third party which ever avariciously tried to reach government except through the regular two-party system.




The party system succeeded, of course, beyond the wildest dreams of its creators. It relegated the founders of the Constitution to the role of doctrinaire theorists, political amateurs. Just because it grew up slowly to meet the needs of ambitious politicians and was not imposed by ruling-class fiat, as was the Constitution, did it have a chance to become assimilated, worked into the political intelligence and instinct of the people, and be adopted gladly and universally as a genuine political form, expressive both of popular need and ruling-class demand. It satisfied the popular demand for democracy. The enormous sense of victory which followed the sweeping away of property qualifications of suffrage, the tangible evidence that now every citizen was participating in public affairs, and that the entire manhood democracy was now self-governing, created a mood of political complacency that lasted uninterruptedly into the twentieth century. The party system was thus the means of removing political grievance from the greater part of the populace, and of giving to the ruling classes the hidden but genuine permanence of control which the Constitution had tried openly to give them. It supplemented and repaired the ineptitudes of the Constitution. It became the unofficial but real government, the instrument which used the Constitution as its instrument.




Only in two cases did the party system seem to lose its grip, was it thrown off base by the inception of a new party from without — in the elections of Jackson and Lincoln. Jackson came in as the representative of a new democratic West which had no tradition of suffrage qualifications, and Lincoln as a minority candidate in a time of factional sectional strife. But the discomfiture of the party politicians was short. The party system proved perfectly capable of assimilating both of these new movements. Jackson’s insurrection was soon captured by the old machinery and fed the slavocracy, and Lincoln’s party became the property of the new bonanza capitalism. Neither Jackson nor Lincoln made the slightest deflection in the triumphal march of the party-system. In practically no other contests has the electorate had for all practical purposes a choice except between two candidates, identical as far as their political role would be as representatives of the significant classes in the State. Campaigns such as Bryan’s, where one of the parties is captured by an element which seeks a real transference of power from the significant to the less significant classes, split the party, and sporadic third party attacks merely throw the scale one way or the other between the big parties, or, if threatening enough, produce a virtual coalition against them.

Dulce et Decorum Est

 (1920)




Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,

Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,

Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs,

And towards our distant rest began to trudge.

Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots,

But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind;

Drunk with fatigue; deaf even to the hoots

Of gas-shells dropping softly behind.




Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!—An ecstasy of fumbling

Fitting the clumsy helmets just in time,

But someone still was yelling out and stumbling

And flound’ring like a man in fire or lime.—

Dim through the misty panes and thick green light,

As under a green sea, I saw him drowning.




In all my dreams before my helpless sight,

He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning.




If in some smothering dreams, you too could pace

Behind the wagon that we flung him in,

And watch the white eyes writhing in his face,

His hanging face, like a devil’s sick of sin;

If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood

Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs,

Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud

Of vile, incurable sores on innocent tongues,—

My friend, you would not tell with such high zest

To children ardent for some desperate glory,

The old Lie: 

Dulce et decorum est

Pro patria mori

 [Horace: It is sweet and fitting to die for one’s country].




Wilfred Owen







Veterans of the US Military in Their Own Words




from the 

CrimethInc.

 collective, 11/11/2026




What is it like to serve in the United States military? If only it were possible for those who are considering enlisting to learn the unvarnished truth. In 2019, a viral 

tweet

 from the official US Army twitter account unexpectedly drew over 11,000 candid replies in the course of 48 hours. These responses offer a rare window into the real experiences of servicemembers and veterans. We present a selection of them here for the benefit of anyone who is thinking about joining the military.




This is a document of an 

earlier era

 of social media, captured here before it 

vanishes

. You can obtain a book collecting the first twenty-four hours of responses 

here

.










Just before Memorial Day in 2019, the United States Army made a strategic blunder almost on par with invading Vietnam. They posted this inquiry on their official Twitter account:







In response, veterans and their family and friends posted thousands upon thousands of tweets recounting broken promises and broken people. They described cancer, PTSD, domestic abuse, unpaid college and housing loans, Gulf War syndrome, insomnia, sexual abuse, poverty, Agent Orange, racism, nightmare disorder, unemployment, burying loved ones, misogyny, orphaned children, burn pit syndrome, homelessness, debilitating injuries, divorce, alcoholism, disappearances, a Veterans Affairs department that was unwilling or unable to help, and suicide, suicide, suicide.




















































The United States military is one of the largest concentrations of power in the world. With 

tens of thousands

 of missiles, 

millions

 of firearms, and over 

5000

 nuclear weapons—about 40% of all the nuclear weapons in the world—the US military can hold the entire world hostage.



















The US military is also the largest employer in the United States, 

employing

 almost 2,900,000 workers—roughly 17 out of every 2000 people. If we add private military contractors like Blackwater (250,000 workers), the employees of non-combat support companies like Halliburton who build military infrastructure, provide food, and the like (150,000-250,000), US-based war manufacturers like Lockheed Martin and Boeing (1,500,000), and 

veterans

 who receive disability or pension payments (2,000,000), we find that roughly 1 out of every 50 Americans is economically dependent on US militarism.




As in all industries, without this workforce, the military would grind to a halt. It especially depends on regular transfusions of young blood—young people sold stories about adventure, duty, and upward mobility.



















If we were to ask new recruits why they joined, we’d 

likely

 hear a mix of narratives about gaining strength, seeing the world, paying for college, serving God and country, learning life skills, continuing a family tradition, escaping poverty or an unsafe home, obtaining housing, having fun, and protecting loved ones. Most people join the military because they think it will benefit them or because they believe they are serving a higher calling.






















Some recruits get to live out their dreams. Some leave instability, danger, or deprivation for a more structured and economically stable life; some even gain a sense of belonging. If they’re lucky, they serve their time without incident, then move on to free college tuition, a no-down-payment housing loan, health insurance, and a free meal at Golden Corral once a year.






















But thousands of veterans’ dreams become nightmares. The promises of recruiters, family members, and Hollywood movies offer a gamble at best—a roll of the dice that 

frequently

 ends with being harmed physically, psychologically, and sexually. Military service can lead to 

substance abuse

, 

homelessness

, and 

suicide

. It can also end in unspeakable acts of violence against others, whether those be the declared enemies of the United States, noncombatants, or veterans’ own loved ones.

























It is striking how many of these responses speak of being hoodwinked out of college, housing loans, and medical care—how many describe the pain of family members lost to PTSD, alcoholism, or suicide after witnessing or committing atrocities.






















American media bombards us with war propaganda. Almost every video game spreads the myth that combat makes us stronger: more powerful weapons, tougher armor, a bigger health bar, greater fortunes. Hollywood promises that the hero can weather any fight—or, if he can’t, his death will be meaningful and glorious.




Statistically speaking, the more we are exposed to combat, the more likely we are to be severely harmed, both physically and 

mentally

. This is true for both 

servicemembers

 and 

civilians

. As for the families we want to protect, at least 

one out of every three

 veterans brings the war home to their family through domestic abuse. Veterans are 

two to four times

 more likely to harm their families than their civilian counterparts.






















After massive troop and draftee 

resistance

 during the late 1960s and early 1970s, the US government ended selective compulsory military service (known as “the draft”). The military transitioned to a volunteer force, which means 

depending on

 recruits from families with a military tradition, working-class and impoverished enlistees, and whomever else recruiters can trick.




As one commenter pointed out,







How many people would give recruiters the time of day if they led with the truth?




“How would you like an 

11-20% chance

 of having debilitating PTSD? Or say, a 

7-11% chance

 of severe physical disability? A 32-50% chance you’ll 

physically

 or 

sexually

 abuse your family? If you’re a woman, I can promise you at least a 

25-50% chance

 that another service member will assault you. Or perhaps you’d like to become one of 

over 32,000 homeless veterans

?”




“But if you want to 

assault civilians

 in another country—to 

kill them and 

mutilate

 their bodies

—the likelihood of you getting in trouble will be 

almost zero.”






















If the benefits are bait to lure the young, the desperate, and the bored, what about the narratives that draw those who seek a higher calling?




Almost every war America has fought in the last hundred years has not achieved its stated goals. Supposedly, the US military invaded Iraq to bring stability, peace, and democracy to the region; in fact, it brought years of civil war and death. Most US citizens still cannot name the current Iraqi head of state or describe the political situation in Iraq. Twenty years of fighting in Afghanistan and Vietnam resulted in the Taliban and Vi?t C?ng acquiring more power than they started with. The Korean War has technically never ended; pick your poison—the poverty and hunger of a communist dictatorship or the sterility, inequality, and exploitation of the modern capitalist world.




We are told that World War II was fought to end authoritarianism and establish global peace. Yet fascism proper remained in power Spain and Portugal, while explicitly white supremacist governments retained control in places like South Africa—and the US government maintained supportive relations with all of them. In the wake of the war, humanity faced the threat of nuclear annihilation in a new Cold War. The military-industrial complex became one of the most powerful forces in society, and all kinds of violent and humiliating forms of oppression continued to exist in the victorious countries as well as the defeated ones.




But at least the Great War—the war fought to end all wars—brought lasting peace to the world. Right?

























War is a racket.

 The rich and powerful use those below them as cannon fodder as they maneuver to acquire more wealth and power. In 2003, the oil reserves of Iraq were the third largest in the world. Shortly after the US invasion and toppling of Saddam Hussein’s government, the reserves were privatized and contracted to Western companies, generating windfall profits for a few lucky capitalists.




A popular anti-war chant at the time exhorted, 

“ExxonMobil, BP, Shell, take your war and go to hell!”

























While militarists justified the War on Terror with rhetoric about fighting evildoers, the Bush administration sought to establish footholds on various continents in order to maintain military dominance throughout the world. One of the reasons the 

Afghan War

 lasted as long as it did is that the military industry prolonged it for profit. The United States government spent 

over $21,000,000,000,000

 on the War on Terror.




Weapons manufacturers made a killing. During the years 2020-2024 alone—in other words, well after the Iraq and Afghanistan wars were over—$771 billion in Pentagon contracts 

went to

 Lockheed Martin ($313 billion), RTX (formerly Raytheon, $145 billion), Boeing ($115 billion), General Dynamics ($116 billion), and Northrop Grumman ($81 billion).


































Even if we set aside the question of how the US government came to have $21 trillion at its disposal in the first place—think about what that $21 trillion spent on the War on Terror could have been used for instead. What do you need to live a happy, fulfilling life? What do the peoples of Iraq and Afghanistan and Vietnam need? How much healthcare and education could have been provided? Genuine healthcare, not what the VA and the for-profit hospitals crank out or deny. And real education—skills people need and want for life, knowledge based on our passions—not the traps that pass for schools in America, one part daycare and one part prison.




But thank goodness the US government didn’t go to the peoples of Iraq and Afghanistan and meet their needs. 

Fundamentalist extremism would surely have ballooned in popularity after that!

























It is not surprising that the US government and the warmongers didn’t meet the needs of the people they claimed to be liberating. They need new terrorists, or at least the threat of new terrorists, to keep up the racket. Without the fear of outsiders menacing America, how would they arrange trillions for war?



















We could tally up who profited on the Vietnam War or World War I with similar results. The protests and revolutions that broke out around the world during and after both of those wars indicate how millions of people understood what those wars were truly about. They showed successive generations that militarism, capitalism, nationalism, and authoritarianism only benefit those at the top.




























Militarism always preys on the young and vulnerable, luring them with tales of heroism, riches, and duty. The young and desperate will serve their countries until they realize that their countries do not serve them.




No governments ever have. None ever will.



















The public can no longer view all of the replies to “How has serving impacted you?” The website still claims to retain 8.7k of them, but they are not accessible. In part, this is because people deleting their accounts, whether out of boredom with the platform or because they don’t want to support Elon Musk’s embrace of techno-fascism.




The X algorithm promotes conservative and extreme-right content, suppresses news from traditional corporate media outlets, and promotes “independent” but usually conservative or far-right influencers. When Elon Musk bought Twitter, he immediately 

purged

 high-profile accounts belonging to anarchists, anti-fascists, and far-left users. All of these are obstacles to using what remains of the platform under his ownership.



















In reaction to the neoconservatives in the Bush administration who led the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, many American conservatives shifted toward paleo-conservatism during the years-running Iraq and Afghanistan Wars. Some even became openly critical of war. Many believed that, in casting votes for Donald Trump, they were electing a politician who would keep the United States out of wars. But wherever there is nationalism, wherever state power is concentrated in the hands of an aspiring autocrat, 

war is never far behind

.




The answers to “How has serving impacted you?” comprise an interracial, multi-generational, gender-inclusive condemnation of the US military that cuts across the political spectrum. This is more of a liability to X’s brand of techno-fascism than an asset. Elon Musk’s platform has not buried them entirely, yet, but it’s not the sort of thing that he and his underlings would want people to easily and completely access. In view of that, it is unusual that so many damning tweets remain—a testament to how dangerous it is to trust your life to the military. It is worth documenting them before they disappear.




If you or your family members are currently serving in the US military, please contact the GI Rights Hotline at 1-877-447-4487 or just go AWOL. There is no need to stay in the service of a violent front for weapons and defense corporations. There’s no reason to die for their benefit, and there’s absolutely no excuse to become complicit in what the US government has done to to the people of Afghanistan, Iraq, and Iran.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The children in revolt
content:
by Francesco Demitry




from 

lundimatin

, #541, 10/11/2026




They learn to wait for the bell, the bus, their turn to speak, permission to go out, for the day someone deems them old enough to understand the world. They learn to become alienated. They learn to keep quiet, to be silent. Then, one morning, they overturn the tables in front of the gate, and the town discovers they exist.







The young people who have occupied the streets in Italy and France in recent weeks are not mere ambassadors of hope, nor are they the innocent mascots of a political establishment running out of words. They are bodies that are hungry, that are cold, that feel anger and desire, that know overcrowded classrooms, dismantled services, and a mortgaged future. In France, the mobilisation began in the Parisian suburbs, where students denounced the deterioration of schools, vacant teaching positions, and the lack of nurses and social workers. It spread to more than a thousand schools across the country. In Italy, students led the marches against the high cost of living, rents, low wages, rearmament, and the war economy. In Genoa, thousands of people entered the port to protest the transit of weapons. Different stories, but on both sides of the Alps, the same melody is emerging: that of a generation rejecting a world it is supposed to inherit, a world that is already closed.




To whom does a school belong without teachers? To whom belongs a city where the bus is too expensive, where housing is becoming unaffordable, where the park is fenced off and the courtyard sold? School is where inequality is laid bare: a crumbling building in a working-class neighborhood, a replacement teacher who never arrives, a closed workshop, a dry tap. Our address should not determine our future, some French high school students have written. Capitalism seeks to transform space into destiny, assigning each person a piece of the city and calling the distance between those who can cross it and those who must remain confined to their neighborhood or be evicted a matter of merit.




Governments respond with budgets and decrees. They announce recruitment and controls, deploy law enforcement. On November 5th, in France, as unions and students took to the streets again to demand better wages, public services, and education, the state deployed a significant security apparatus. In Italy, a few days earlier, police water cannons had dispersed a march in Turin. Faced with people forging their own path, the authorities presented the bill: order. But a public square is not a classroom that can simply be brought into line. The square is overflowing; it is bursting at the seams. Those who are protesting cannot simply be asked to raise their hands and wait for their demands to be reviewed by the appropriate department.




Luis Buñuel found an extraordinary image of how a social class, that of the old petty bourgeoisie, manages to survive everything; even the disintegration of the world around it. In 

The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie

, six characters are constantly trying to sit down at the table, to have a meal, to re-establish the small order of their habits. But something intervenes each time to interrupt them: a corpse, an army, the police, a story of violence, a dream that invades reality. The world knocks on the dining room door, and dinner is inevitably postponed. And the most disturbing thing is not that these people continue to desire their meal, but that each catastrophe seems incapable of changing anything in their lives. The bourgeoisie possesses this extraordinary capacity: to absorb interruption, to transform conflict into an annoyance, a minor inconvenience, history into a conversation that must be interrupted, always with decorum. Even when everything falls apart, the napkin is folded, the glass refilled, the appointment postponed. But it is above all in 

The Phantom of Liberty

 that Buñuel pushes this intuition to its most radical consequences. A group of bourgeois is invited to dinner and cordially ushered around a table surrounded by toilets. The guests sit down, lower their trousers, relieve themselves, and, in the meantime, smoke while conversing amiably. They talk about travel, current events, social conventions, without anyone seeming to find anything strange about the situation. The indecency, if there is any in this scene, lies elsewhere: in the act of eating. When they are hungry, the guests discreetly withdraw to a small room to eat their meal alone, discreetly asking where the kitchen is, with the same shame as if they were trying to conceal something improper. In a matter of minutes, Buñuel overturns the entire edifice of convention: what civilization considers private becomes public, what is celebrated as a ritual of conviviality becomes a practice to be concealed. This is not mere provocation, but a radical critique of the social construction of decorum, of the artificial separation between the body and its representation, between material needs and the forms by which a society decides to make them acceptable. Eating and defecating belong to the same material continuity of life, but the bourgeois order distributes them into different spaces, times, and hierarchies, establishing what can be shown and what must be hidden. The body, with its needs, its biology, and its excesses, becomes something to be administered, disciplined, and, above all, made presentable.




Is not this one of the first operations by which children are educated? Proper posture, not getting dirty, not shouting, not touching, not running, asking permission, learning to control every bodily action. School thus becomes a small factory of decorum, where even vitality must learn to occupy its assigned space and respect a predetermined time. Children who disrupt this order are not simply disobeying the rules: for a few moments, they make visible the body that the social order seeks to domesticate.




This is why their revolt is so dangerous: they do not want to be invited to this table, do not ask to take their place, do not demand a larger portion of the same meal. None of that. Their revolt disrupts the ritual and reveals its violence. They ask who built this room, who set the table, who cooks, who stays behind the door. They don’t want to sit at the table, but to rearrange the house and leave.




Artaud sought in the body a language withdrawn from the control of the masters. Young people find it again in dissonant choruses, footsteps that disrupt traffic, painted placards, overlapping voices, even in battles of aura. The body in the street produces and imposes the programme, tests it, transforms it. Michaux would have recognised in these signs an unstable geography, a writing made of shifts, stains, and inventions. The protest has neither a center nor a phrase that can summarise it. It is made up of a multitude of gestures seeking a polyphonic composition: who holds the banner, who distributes water, who brings Maalox, who stops in front of a police cordon, who returns the next day, who joins the workers’ procession, who participates from afar.




Gianni Rodari

 knew that imagination is not a pastime that adults grant children once their homework is done. It is a political faculty that allows us to overturn words, to change the rules of the game, to discover that the world could have been built differently. In his grammar, error can become invention, an unexpected combination can open a path, an absurd question can reveal and dismantle the absurdity of habitual answers.




But what would happen if we applied this lesson to the city? What if, instead of teaching children to adapt to available spaces, we allowed them to invent others? What if the closed gate became a door, the abandoned lot a garden, the street a meeting place?




Children are not subjects unfamiliar with rules, but rather those who can demonstrate how contingent they are; and sometimes, how unjust they are.




Here, 

Colin Ward

 becomes an important ally. The city is also what children make of sidewalks, abandoned lots, and the passageways between buildings. Play is a practice of appropriating the world, an ability to organise oneself without waiting for permission.

[1]

 Nietzsche explained that we must relate to the world with the same seriousness as a child at play. Taking children seriously means recognising their political power and competence: forging alliances, inventing provisional rules, transforming a place, and caring for those left behind. When students block the school gate, the question must be what can be done together outside of the intended and pre-established use of this space.




There is another cinematic alliance I would like to mention: that of Harold and Maude in Hal Ashby’s film [of the same name]. Harold is a young man from a wealthy and privileged family, surrounded by objects, opportunities, and attention that never reach him (or from which he escapes). He constantly stages his own death, as if only the representation of the end could make visible an existence that others do not see. His mother, a bourgeois woman, tries to correct him by entrusting him to “experts” and attempting to make him respectable through marriage and social conventions. But then Maude, a woman approaching eighty, arrives unexpectedly, seemingly from another world. Maude attends funerals, steals cars, listens to music, indulges her desires, runs away and mocks the police, uproots a tree from the asphalt and carries it into the forest, returning it to a land where it can continue to grow. She does not want to teach Harold how to become a respectable adult, but shows him that it is still possible to let life flow through him, that there are encounters capable of reawakening the senses, that the world is by no means a possession to be kept, but a material to be transformed. Their alliance is based neither on resemblance nor on mutual reassurance. Together, they create an experience that neither of them could have generated alone. One generation can influence the other, reactivate its desires, open unexpected pathways. Maude takes Harold out of his home and returns the world to him as a sensory experience. And this tree replanted in the forest becomes more than an ecological gesture: it demonstrates that a life can be rescued from its assigned destiny and placed within a different network of relationships. It is about making possible again what does not yet exist.




Italo Calvino bequeathed to us cities that cannot be reduced to their walls, their monuments, their owners. Cities made of desires, memories, encounters, invisible relationships. 

Invisible Cities

 inhabit the possibilities that a real city contains but that its economic order prevents from being realised. Every neighbourhood could be another neighbourhood, every street could lead to an encounter rather than a parking lot, every empty space could become the site of a shared life. The lightness that Calvino offers is the gesture of one who manages to free the world from the weight of hierarchies, to imagine passages where power has chosen to build walls for its own benefit. Children do this constantly because they have not yet accepted that the harshness of the world, of which they are nonetheless aware, is the only thing that is possible one.




And there is something else that adults have taught children: time. Everything must be in its place; every activity has its appointed time; every desire is postponed until the opportune moment. The day is divided into segments, the body trained for punctuality, curiosity interrupted by the sound of the bell. We tell them that play must find its place in the schedule, as if it were a break from real life, the one in which we are (and must remain) immersed. Yet, it is precisely in this break that something escapes the measurement of production. A child can spend an entire afternoon (a lifetime) following an ant or a stream, inventing a city with three cardboard boxes or empty water bottles, following a path that leads nowhere. In economic terms, this means producing nothing. But that is wrong. On the contrary, the child produces relationships, discoveries, possibilities, and a quantity (and quality) of world that no indicator could ever quantify.




It’s also a question of time subtracted. Families have to rush to work, juggle schedules, pay for services that replace time spent caring, and be exasperated by children’s insistent demands. Teachers have to fill out forms, chase deadlines, and respond to administrative procedures. And the children? They must learn early, as early as possible, to be efficient, independent, and competitive, so as not to burden the bureaucratic and efficient organisation of real life. Life is thus constantly prepared, organised, and postponed. But when exactly does this life begin? When does the preparation finally end, and when does the right to inhabit the world begin? At what time? The promise of a better future becomes a perverse form of discipline, used to demand and justify the sacrifices of the present. Young people are told that one day they will be able to choose, provided that today they learn to obey. Their eruption into the streets challenges us and shatters this temporal blackmail. They are not simply asking for a different future: they are clamouring for a present where it is possible to live differently.




The children in revolt are the high school students in the streets and the children staring at closed shop windows, the striking workers, the parents struggling to make ends meet. They are the inhabitants of neighbourhoods without gardens, of villages where schools are closing, of territories ravaged by factories or highways. They are those who are asked to adapt to an increasingly uninhabitable planet. They are told that adaptation is a virtue, not a polite way of surrendering. Their revolt turns the question on its head: how do we dismantle the world that prevents them from truly inhabiting it?




Let us not, however, make the mistake of thinking that this would mean replacing adult politics with a children’s politics, as if two separate worlds existed and one had to finally take the place of the other. Revolt does not need a new identity to preserve, a chosen generation, or a savior figure come to redeem past defeats. Its movement is, fortunately, more unpredictable. A teenager blocking their school, a parent defending time for care, a teacher in a precarious situation, a worker going on strike, a resident preventing the overdevelopment of their neighbourhood can all recognise themselves in the same struggle without sharing the same history, the same language, or the same vision of the future. They do not need to become alike to find common ground. They must be able to mutually transform their possibilities.




An alliance is neither the sum of pre-existing interests, nor an agreement between organisations that decide to support each other. It is rather an encounter that transforms those who take part, unleashing previously nonexistent capacities. When student mobilisation meets workers’ strikes, when the right to education is intertwined with the right to housing, when the fight against war meets the struggle for territorial defence, it is not simply a matter of adding demands to a checklist. What changes is the way we perceive the conflict. What appears to be an individual problem reveals itself, as always, to be a social relationship. What seems like a simple local issue demonstrates its connection to a much larger economic machine.




This is why it is not enough to ask ourselves what children lack (resources, infrastructure, teachers, green spaces, time, affection…). Their presence cannot be understood through a kind of “catalogue of deprivations”. Desire, once again, does not arise from a void that someone should finally fill. Desire is revolutionary because it has the capacity to encounter, to combine, to build. An occupied courtyard, a communal kitchen, a school open to the neighbourhood, a garden rescued from neglect are not temporary responses to a lack, but genuine creations of reality, capable of bringing into being relationships that were previously nonexistent, of transforming a space, of generating new shared imaginaries. Revolt also begins in this way, when a possibility ceases to be merely conceived and becomes a practice.




And there can be no ecology without this capacity. Children are told that they must protect nature separate from the city, that they must recycle and turn off the lights, while adults continue to organise extraction, consumption, exploitation, and destruction. Ecology is not a virtuous behaviour to be added to the school curriculum, perhaps during extracurricular hours or dedicated subjects. Ecology is a question of the relationships between human beings and other forms of life, between bodies and environments, between those who decide the fate of a territory and those who are forced to endure it. What does it mean to talk about the future to a child growing up beside a polluted road, in a treeless suburb, in a territory where water is privatised or land is given over to speculation? The ecological crisis is not a distant threat. It is already distributed, in space and in bodies, according to a very precise class geography.




The children’s revolt connects the school with the river, the playground with the forest, the port with the neighbourhood, because children know that no form of life can be isolated from the relationships that make it possible. It is a politics of interdependence, a practice of alliance between heterogeneous worlds. A felled tree, a dried-up spring, an animal driven from its habitat—these too tell a story about this same world order that would have students silent and adults docile. There is no external environment that needs saving after society has been put back in order. Society is already an environment, made up of bodies, infrastructure, emotions, dependencies, and conflicts.




Perhaps we need a clandestine approach to possibility, in the sense of wresting life from prescribed destinies by reopening this administered future, which we treat as an already exhausted possibility. We must preserve a shared possibility at the heart of the catastrophe. We must not ask children to save us. Entrusting them with the weight (and the guilt) of our absolution would be the ultimate form of exploitation. Instead, let us ask that their presence transform our way of deciding, producing, and inhabiting. Revolt is life taking up space, here and now, in this very moment. If the streets are filling up again, it is because diverse bodies, often at odds, have discovered that they can walk together without becoming alike.




The city belongs neither to those who govern it nor to those who buy it. It belongs to those who traverse it, care for it, disrupt it, and reinvent it. One morning, the children overturn the tables, open the gates, and occupy the sidewalk. And the city, which wanted them in line, is forced, for a moment, to learn from them the most difficult verb: to begin.







[1]

 [T.N. See: Colin Ward,  

The Child in the City

 (1978), 

The Anarchist Library

.]

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: Political elections or opinion polls?
content:
Auguste Couder, 

Le Serment du Jeu de Paume, 20 juin 1789

. 1848







The fact that what we continue to call democracy has lost its meaning is demonstrated by the indiscriminate use of opinion polls, which lay bare the already obvious fact that elections are merely a survey of public opinion rather than an expression of political will. Opinion polls, by showing day by day—through fluctuations in respondents’ views—the numerical standing of the parties, carry out a sort of continuous election, which nobody controls and which can therefore, as indeed happens, be manipulated to in turn influence the very opinion it is supposed to reflect. We call democracy a government of public opinion; that is to say, of something politically entirely insubstantial, which has no reality other than the polls, which, at the very moment they appear to record it, create, alter and manipulate it incessantly. The process by which Rousseau’s 

volonté générale

 [general will]—which cannot be quantified—has gradually been transformed into public opinion, which is merely a matter of numbers, defines the fate of Western democracies.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The Hot Potato Changes Hands Again
content:
On the 2026 Midterm Elections




from the 

CrimethInc. 

collective, 06/11/2026




Ultimately, the Democrats are no more capable of addressing the root causes of popular anger than the Republicans. State power will continue to swing back and forth more and more wildly between different parties until our rulers consolidate an autocracy or we manage to effect revolutionary change.










As we anticipated 

in April

, the death knell of the Trump era has rung. Despite being 

historically unpopular

, Democratic politicians won a sweeping victory in the November 2026 midterm elections. Many are describing the rout as an “

extinction-level event

” for the Republican Party.




All this should feel familiar. Only two years ago, when Democrats lost the 2024 elections, pundits across the political spectrum rushed to declare the collapse of the Democratic Party. Summarizing a widespread perception, one 

expert

 claimed that







“Fundamental shifts are occurring in the body politic that have left Democrats on the wrong side of the popular vote, congressional races, and the country’s shifting demographics.”







Two years later, people are saying the same things about the Republican Party. The backlash against Republicans in this year’s election eclipses the gains they made in 2024. Yet the pendulum has been swinging wildly back and forth between parties for over a decade now—and it could be that the wildest swings have yet to come.




For all the talk of political polarization, loyalty to political parties is at its 

lowest

 in decades. Since at least 2016, anger at the status quo has been the most powerful force in politics; Democrats like Hillary Clinton and Joe Biden who attempted to present themselves as its defenders have learned that the hard way. Likewise, Donald Trump has only able to win elections when he is not in office. Whenever Trump represents the ruling order, he draws the same backlash that he once managed to channel.




Since 2014, we have argued that state power itself has become a hot potato that burns whoever holds it. In a globalized economy, in which governments can no longer mitigate the impact of capitalism on their citizens without investors taking their money elsewhere, no party is able to hold state power for long without losing credibility with voters. Similarly, the challenges of maintaining position as a waning imperial power inevitably undercut the legitimacy of whoever controls the state: just as the genocide in Gaza damaged the Biden administration’s support, Trump’s 

war with Iran

 has contributed to driving away voters.




Similar things are taking place all around the world. 

British politicians

 have also seen rapid reversals in fortune. The centrist parties that have long ruled Germany and France are in precipitous decline. One Latin American government after another has swung to the far right, but that hardly indicates a 

social consensus

 in favor of 

any political camp

.




Only countries under continuous autocratic rule, such as Russia, Belarus, China, and North Korea, are excepted from the hot potato pattern. Donald Trump has made no secret of his desire to establish a similar state of affairs in the United States. Yet even in Hungary, which Republicans took as a model for their illiberal aspirations, the long-running autocratic government ultimately lost control. The same has occurred in Poland and, more recently, Serbia. Wherever voters have an opportunity—however narrow—to demand change, they do so—however arbitrarily and capriciously.




With no prospect of improving life for his rank-and-file supporters, Trump’s solution was to 

inflict violence

 on their behalf, offering them the vicarious thrill of watching the state cause harm to others as an outlet for their frustration. 

Less bread, more circuses

.




Republicans and Democrats—trash and recycling.




It might have worked—if ordinary people had not courageously taken the streets to interfere. We owe Trump’s failure to those who assembled at 

Tesla dealerships

 in spring 2025, who 

rose up

 against federal agents and the National Guard that June, who confronted Immigration and Customs Enforcement mercenaries in 

Chicago

, 

Minnesota

, and elsewhere. As we previously saw in 

the movement against police and white supremacy

, when people take risks in solidarity with others, this makes it possible for more people to experience empathy where previously, they only felt dissociation and apathy.




The grassroots resistance that emerged in response to the Trump administration stands in stark contrast to the way that elite figures across the political spectrum immediately put themselves as Trump’s disposal. Tech billionaires from Silicon Valley flocked to his inauguration to throw themselves at his feet. Powerful 

law firms

, university administrations, and 

corporations

 subordinated themselves to his will. Heads of state from across the world groveled and toadied to Trump—regardless of how he 

treated

 them, no matter how absurd his 

demands

.




Throughout 2025, Democratic politicians confined themselves to expressing opposition in purely symbolic ways, if occasionally 

at great length

. Cowardly centrist Democrats had already 

embraced Trump’s anti-immigrant politics

 well before the 2024 election; after it, many of them 

actively participated

 in the Trump regime’s attacks on immigrants, seizing the opportunity to call for the Democratic Party to continue tacking 

rightward

.




The scale of subsequent 

resistance

 to ICE showed that this was not hard-nosed pragmatism, but political opportunism at the service of xenophobia. A 

poll

 at the beginning of March 2026 showed that only 39% of respondents opposed abolishing ICE, with fully 50% actively calling for its abolition. The disparity between these figures and the very small number of politicians prepared to consider abolishing ICE even today shows that Democratic politicians will openly defy their supporters’ wishes in order to continue to advance a reactionary agenda. As politicians, they do not simply answer to a constituency of voters, but above all to a clientele of capitalists.




Trump did his best to rig the system in his favor ahead of the 2026 elections, arranging for widespread gerrymandering, seeking to control the voting process, and attempting to put the pieces in place to contest the results. Billionaires backed him financially—Elon Musk singlehandedly spent half a billion dollars, a quarter of the entire Republican budget for the election, in an effort to put his thumb on the scales. In the end, the results were so conclusive that none of this mattered. As in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the majority of voters rejected the reigning party.




Yet because this will was expressed via voting, rather than through more direct means, the result simply hands power to another coterie of politicians who will not address the needs of those who elected them. The more secure the Democrats’ grip on power becomes, the less they will concern themselves with the wishes of the electorate. If anything, the 2026 election will only embolden the centrists within the party, as it put power in the hands of more moderate Democrats, especially in swing districts.




But those who imagine that the Democrats did so well in the 2026 election on their own merits are fooling themselves.




The core issue at the root of the hot potato pattern is that the existing political order cannot address the instability, disparities, and crises of a capitalist system that has concentrated most of the wealth of society in the hands of a few while inflicting grievous social, psychological, and ecological damage on the rest of us. No political party will initiate the kind of revolutionary transformation that will be required to shift to a more egalitarian and sustainable way of life; such change can only come from grassroots mobilization. As long as there is no widespread, powerful social movement that offers the prospect of addressing these problems through profound change, people will continue rejecting one government after another in increasing desperation.




Silicon Valley tech moguls—who backed Joe Biden in 2020 only to switch sides in 2024—are even less popular than Donald Trump. Hatred of tech billionaires, data centers, and Flock cameras cuts across political lines; like the war on Iran, it is one of the factors that caused many former Trump voters to stay home or vote for Democrats. Yet as they regain their hold on power, Democrats will be inclined to work more and more closely with capitalists and the tech industry, rhetoric about “oligarchy” notwithstanding.







If social movements die down again as they did in 2021 after Biden took office, this will bode ill for the future, opening the way for even more extreme far-right reactionaries to pretend that they represent the only alternative to an unendurable status quo. If the 

cycle

 that played out between the first and second Trump administrations repeats itself again, the third iteration of far-right reaction will be more horrific than we can possibly imagine.




For good or ill, it does not look like anyone will be able to delude themselves into believing in a “return to normal” any time soon. The 

accession

 of Stephen Miller, an avowed white supremacist, to White House Chief of Staff sets the stage for the Trump administration to conclude with a period of brutal, open conflict. The administration lacks the support to win an open power struggle with the rest of society, but has left itself no alternative. As one 

New York Times

 commentator put it, “The next two years could actually be pretty volatile.”




As long as Trump remains in power, the far right will be perceived as the hegemonic force against which social anger will gravitate. But we must not wait for Democratic politicians to stand up to the Trump administration; even if they did, at best, that would function to relegitimize the same state institutions that will once again be turned against us in the future—as we saw in the Democrats’s response to the 

failed coup

 of January 6, 2021.




We must set an example by continuing to resist the Trump administration—and, wherever necessary, Democratic local and state administrations as well—through grassroots 

direct action

. Rather than simply waging a defensive struggle, we must figure out how to take proactive steps towards 

a completely different way of life

 in the process. Otherwise, the far right will eventually benefit once again from the inevitable disillusionment with Democratic administrations.




At best, the election results should function as a mandate for grassroots resistance to the Trump administration’s policies, not as a pressure valve for anxiety about them. We must build the grassroots capacity to defend and care for our communities. If we succeed, Democratic politicians will probably try to co-opt whatever we have achieved by offering to do the same things for us through the state. But they will only offer us what we demonstrate the ability to accomplish ourselves, and it is better to develop the ability to address needs directly and consistently than for the well-being of our communities to depend on the outcome of elections.




In short: it’s good to see Trump losing control. But the pendulum will continue to swing back and forth between political parties in wilder and wilder oscillations until we make revolutionary changes in our society.

Woodcut by Frans Masereel







from Peter Gelderloos’ substack page, 

Suviving Leviathan

, 05/11/2026







Breathing Room




from the apocalyptic, fascistic Right to the insufficient, hypocritical, quietly genocidal Left




In the recent elections in Brasil, one of the largest countries in the Global South, leftwing darling Lula beat Flavio Bolsonaro, the fascistic dynast supported by the country’s plantation owner class. In Israel, the extreme Right lost the elections to the far Right (not a typo). And in the US, a “blue wave” has given the Democrats an ample margin of control in both chambers of Congress as well as a strong majority of governorships (for non-US readers, for whatever weird-ass reason related to our especially amnesiac, isolationist culture, in the US blue is the color of the Left and red is the color of the Right). In once Republican-held or toss-up states like Texas, North Carolina, and New Jersey, Democratic candidates won by double digits while conservatives won in what were, until yesterday, solidly Republican states like Florida or Louisiana by only 1 or 2%.







A high level Republican operative connected to Trump admitted to the press that these elections were just “too big to rig,” casually acknowledging how common it is to redraw electoral maps or send the precise vote-counting machines to the friendly districts and low quality, high-failure-rate machines to the unfriendly districts, in order to win an extra percentage point and tip elections.




Brasil




In Brasil, where former far Right president Jair Bolsonaro serves a sentence of house arrest in his mansion for launching a failed coup attempt after he lost the 2022 elections, his son Flavio Bolsonaro carried the first round of the elections in early October but failed to attain a majority. In the second round, held October 25

th

, voters turned to the Left and re-elected the incumbent, Lula, off the Workers’ Party. Wealthy investors punished the country for their vote, with the Brasilian stock market taking a plunge after the election even though Lula is a very business-friendly politician who has overseen a large deal of growth and “development” in the Brasilian economy. In practice that means he promotes oil drilling and mining in the Amazon, he subsidizes the intertwined beef-soy industry causing so much destruction in the south and west of the country, and he also supports manufacture and higher tech industry.







Brasil’s stock market index, with the big crash on the right-hand side occurring on October 25.







If Bolsonaro’s son Flavio had won this past 25

th

 of October, the death squads that work for the ranchers, soy plantation owners, miners, loggers, or directly for the state, would have had free rein. Several of my friends and many of the 

Indigenous

, 

African diasporic

, and lower class mestizo or white people 

I met last year

, people at the forefront of 

rural

 and 

urban struggles

 against the ongoing violence of colonial capitalism and 

for a better world

, would have been at greater risk of getting murdered for their resistance. For sure, a lot of people are breathing a very valid sigh of relief. But they’re not naïve about the meaning of the leftwing victory.




[Some of those links above go to 

Antimidia

 videos in Portuguese. Before pressing play, scroll down to “Legendas” and you’ll see buttons for English subtitles.]




As one friend put it, “

If Bolsonaro wins, they kill us; if Lula wins, they let us die.

” A second friend referred to a “mono-polarization” in which there are not two competing poles, just a single pole, “the extreme Right, which pulls everything into its proximity.”




Another friend described the following:







“Bolsonarismo already won. I don’t say that just because the Congress and Senate are controlled by fascists, I’m referring to Lula’s campaign replicating the methods of communication that are very close to fascism (including the name “Lula’s Army”). A few days ago on TV, Lula openly defended lowering the age at which children can be tried as adults (in order to appease the Right) and other similar things. Every time there is a “vote against fascism” which includes the attempt to also convince the Right or “center right,” the pendulum moves to the right.




“After the conservative reaction to 

the 2013 revolt

, some people (like the author Paulo Arantes) said that we were living in a situation with a horizon of diminishing expectations, without a view towards amplifying the struggles and the capacity to dream of a new world. It seems to me that now it’s worse: not only are they [the Left] slamming on the breaks, but the vital energy to struggle was channeled into the methods of the enemy.




“Perhaps what most calls my attention is how the argument for a “struggle for national sovereignty” was adopted in a terrible way. To combat Trump’s intervention pushing for a brutal extractivism to get so-called rare earth minerals, it is affirmed that [these lands and resources] are exclusively Brasilian, as though the problem were only who gets to destroy the Earth and not the destruction itself.”







And a fourth friend shared with a fair amount of alarm and heartbreak over how Lula’s campaign capitalized on the fear of Bolsonaro to break the sense of autonomy of a great many people in one of the strongest, most radical anticolonial and anticapitalist projects in the territories occupied by the Brasilian state. It even got so bad that some comrades accused those who refused to vote of secretly being Bolsonaro supporters.













This quote is from a message they sent me just before the election: “We’ll keep fighting, whoever wins. But here the possible re-election of Lula is referred to as a defeat of Bolsonarismo, and it’s nothing of the kind.”







They also recommended some texts, 

this one is an academic article

 in English, Portuguese, and Spanish about the People’s Web, an anticolonial “land back” network of communities based on direct action, mutual aid, and autonomy, and these two, which are in Spanish, address “

What Do They Mean When They Say Sovereignty?

” and “

Lands Without Borders, Owners, and Flags in Brasil and Argentina

.”







Friends, strangers, comrades, neighbors: we have been making this mistake for too fucking long. Literally millions of us have died in this struggle. We have to get smarter than binary thinking. 

If we can only consider two different options for our world, both of them are Death.

 Fuck antifascism, fuck anti-imperialism, and fuck the democrats, liberals, and Marxists who manipulate those concepts, if all they come to mean is that we have to support a slightly gentler form of colonialism, of white supremacy, of ecocide, of patriarchy. The slower path to Hell still takes you to Hell and, look around folks! We’ve arrived. False pragmatism and the extremely simple-minded strategy of “you have to vote for A because B is worse” have failed us catastrophically. Why on earth would we keep using a strategy that has brought us to this hellscape?




Other worlds are possible, they are already and still alive here in the cracks of the present system, and we desperately need to remember them, imagine them, believe in them, commit to them, and fight for them.




Israel




Let’s turn to the Israeli elections as a great example of the problem of supporting the lesser evil.




For Netanyahu and his colleagues, Arabic people voting in Israel is an existential “emergency.”




In Israel, 11 parties won seats in the Knesset. Nine of those parties are rightwing. The two leftwing parties won only 6% of the vote. And one of those parties (Democrats) isn’t even anti-genocide – they want to stop the ongoing wars and land theft but not necessarily to reverse the land theft and ethnic cleansing Israel is based on. The other, the Joint List, is led by Palestinians who have never been allowed to join the Israeli government. This was, truly, an election between the extreme Right and the far Right. The Opposition coalition won 48 seats in the Knesset, 40 of which are divided amongst three rightwing parties, and 8 of which belong to the only Israeli leftwing party. (Yep! That means that of the Israeli [non-Arabic] part of the electorate, less than 8% vote for the Left, and the rest vote for the far Right or extreme Right.)




The primary campaign promise of the Opposition coalition, led by Gadi Eisenkot’s Yasher party, was to remove Netanyahu from power, not because of all his wars and genocide, but because he’s not doing a great job at those wars and genocide. Polling consistently shows that 

the vast majority of Israelis

 are 

in favor of the genocide

 and 

the wars against Lebanon, Syria, and Iran

, but majorities were 

upset with Netanyahu

 that his government did not 

win the release of the prisoners held by Hamas

 quickly enough and that the methods being used by West Bank settlers 

might lead to more sanctions

 and a loss of support from “the international community” (Europe and the US). Also, many are miffed that *Haredi or Ultra-Orthodox Jews have 

historically been exempted

 from obligatory military service; they want all Israeli citizens to participate in the military. Others are upset with the fact that Netanyahu is avoiding a prison sentence by staying in office. He got convicted, not for war crimes, but for a pretty clear case of corruption.




*(Haredi make up a significant number of the 800,000 settlers living illegally—but with the full support of the state—in the West Bank and East Jerusalem on recently stolen land, and the political parties representing them are a part of Netanyahu’s coalition. To be clear, the Ultra-Orthodox are often the vanguard of the genocide as they attack, burn, plunder, and murder in the West Bank, they just don’t put on a uniform to do it. 

The number of West Bank settlers has roughly doubled in the last 20 years

.)




The second major promise made by the Opposition was to maintain the official, white supremacist tradition in Israeli politics and not to let any Arabic-led party into the government. Since Netanyahu’s party, Likud, still got the most votes (though they lost 9 seats in the Knesset and their ultra-nationalist allies lost a cumulative 5 seats), the only way for the Opposition to keep both of those promises is to rule with a minority coalition that does not include the two Palestinian-led parties but relies on their votes for investiture and critical legislation, which means a really solid practice of compromise. That shouldn’t be so difficult. Both of those parties have said they would do whatever it takes to get rid of Netanyahu and stop some of the more extreme new settlement projects in the West Bank.




That shouldn’t be too hard a compromise. After all, the rightwing Opposition wants to get rid of Netanyahu, and they’re okay with stopping some settlement projects since those empower their political competitors in the Orthodox camp and could hurt their economy by leading to more sanctions. The only thing that could stop them from winning control of the government is their own racism. So… I give them a 50/50 shot, at best. 

Recent polls support that kind of pessimism.

: incredibly few Israelis believe any land should be given back to the Palestinians* or that recently built settlements should be dismantled. They don’t believe the settlements are wrong, but 50% said the policy of land theft and construction in the West Bank should be “adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation”. Amongst Netanyahu’s bloc, however, a solid majority said “the government should continue the policy ‘whatever the price’.” 52% of those polled said they could accept sanctions on individual settlers who were especially violent, but 63% opposed international sanctions being placed on goods coming from illegal settlements (“illegal,” in the media, referring to Palestinian lands stolen since the Oslo accords of 1993, not all the land stolen before that). With very few exceptions, most Israelis only oppose the daily violence of settlers in the West Bank if it might hurt them personally. As 

The Guardian

 put it: “The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.”




[*Some Israeli politicians do support giving desert lands, much of it the traditional territory of Bedouins, to Palestinians as a non-consensual exchange to permanently take over more fertile Palestinian lands.]







The bullet and the ballot to keep Palestinians down. Invaders vote at an official polling station set up in the West Bank.







Here’s more detail from other polls. 

In May 2024

, after 7 months of the war on Gaza, only 4% of Israelis thought the country’s assault had gone too far, half thought Israel should directly govern Gaza after the war, and only 8% thought that the people of Gaza should be allowed to choose their own government. By that point, 

Israel had directly killed over 35,000 Palestinians in Gaza

, not counting increased deaths from disease or hunger, they had seriously injured 80,000, and forced 1.7 million out of their homes – completely destroying most of the homes along with all the belongings in them. Over 90% of Israelis thought that was the right thing to do. Actually, that’s incorrect. Half the Israelis polled thought the genocide “had not gone far enough”.




Another year of genocide didn’t soften that view. In August 2025, a poll carried out by an Israeli organization found that 76% of Israelis believed that “

there are no innocents in Gaza

,” tacitly approving of the mass murder of children and noncombatants. The poll was conducted “amid rising racist attacks against Palestinians in occupied territories and Palestinian citizens of Israel.”




An August 2026 poll found that the Israeli public supported the wars against Iran, Lebanon, and Syria, but were “

dissatisfied with the results

,” namely the failure to achieve regime-change in Iran and the slowdowns (so-called ceasefires that the Israeli military violates multiple times every day) in the invasions of Lebanon and Syria. A March 2026 poll published by the 

Times of Israel

 found that 

78% of Israelis supported the war against Iran

 (which at that point had killed at least 1,500 Iranian civilians and an unknown number of Iranian soldiers). Even half of Israelis who identified themselves as leftwing supported the war.







Actually, this isn’t Lebanon, it’s “Greater Israel.”







In conclusion, elections, democracy, and the Left won’t stop Israel’s genocide and ongoing wars because:







the vast majority of Israelis are pro-genocide




even the Left is pro-genocide and half of the Left is pro-war




the Israeli leftwing party only got 6% of the vote, which was a huge gain for them.

The US




The sweeping victory of the Democrats in yesterday’s election illustrates a point I was trying to make in “

The Right’s Rollercoaster to Hell

.” By huffing the fumes of their own ideology of power too deeply, by zealously attacking anyone they perceive as a threat to the established order, the Right frequently damage the basis of their own power. And, at least in the anglosphere, the Right have not had intelligent strategists since the days of Margaret Thatcher and Henry Kissinger. Since then, they’ve just been getting dumber and dumber.




Many people have gotten furious with the rightwing attacks: people who need abortions, people who need access to healthcare, trans folks who want to be treated like people, Black folks who need an end to centuries of lynching, exclusion, and exploitation, Muslims sick of being portrayed as terrorists and invaders, latinas and African immigrants who were being attacked regardless of their status, and all the people who don’t belong to those groups but have loved ones who are, or all those who oppose bigotry and oppression on principle. (Basically, all those whom moderate Democrats refer to as fringe groups or the “woke.”




Then there’s the fact that the stupidity of the Trump regime was wrecking the US economy. While the billionaires keep raking it in, the dollar has lost about 9% of the value it had at the beginning of 2024, 

real wages have been stagnating or falling

, 

underemployment is high

, 

groceries have been getting more expensive

, 

food insecurity, electricity, and gas prices are all going up

, 

rent has increased 44% since 2019

 and 

mortgage rates are almost three times as high

 as they were in 2021. Obviously, all those things are much harder on working class and lower income people, while the rich don’t even notice the price of gas and groceries.




So again, it’s no surprise that most people wanted a big change. This map, showing how far to the left or right the vote went compared with 2024, is a pretty clear illustration.







Three short red arrows showing the districts that shifted a little to the right. Hundreds of long blue arrows showing all the districts that moved far to the left.










Incidentally, the US stock market

 surged 

after the leftwing victory. Remember how the opposite occurred in Brasil? The market has no

 invisible hand

, and there’s no cutthroat, mercenary competition intrinsic to human nature. It’s evil rich fuckers who want Brasil to maintain itself as a plantation for the global economy, where the millionaire landowners and mine owners can easily pay cops or paramilitaries to murder labor organizers or Indigenous people who might get in the way of their investments. The very same banks, corporate execs, and multimillionaire or billionaire investors want the US to maintain a more complex economy with a huge market to import goods from around the world alongside a well educated class of researchers who can be subsidized to develop pharmaceutical, chemical, alternative energy, and computing technologies that will result in trillions of dollars of profits. But a poorer population and major cuts to research subsidies can’t sustain that kind of economy. Clearly, the State is more powerful than capitalists on their own and the capitalists don’t always get their first choice, but they’ll make do with their second. They’ll profit in Brasil under Lula, and they’re happy that things in the US are turning around but if the most powerful government in the world goes too far Left or too far Right or just too far stupid, the capitalists will take their investments elsewhere and a new coalition of powerful states will arise to uphold the global order once NATO can’t hack it. They’re already in the wings, preparing. But maybe there’s another sort of change that could happen…







With a solid majority in Congress, the Democrats will get the opportunity to pass a budget next year that they could use to defund ICE, end military aid to Israel, and restore money to public education, scientific research, and social services related to healthcare, food poverty, and support for disabled people. They can also investigate corruption in the Trump administration, ICE conspiracies to murder or otherwise violate the rights of immigrants and rapid response people, and other instances of law breaking by government officials. And if they don’t fuck it up, they’ll probably win the presidency and keep a congressional majority in 2028.




What’s more, 

progressive candidates swept a number of elections

, including in toss-up states and districts, disproving the rhetoric of the Party establishment that more voters will support moderates and leftwing candidates can’t win competitive elections. That means there’s a possibility for the party as a whole to support more progressive policies by 2028, though of course the 

New York Times

 is scrounging for any statistical manipulation or talking head or can claim the elections were a vindication of the moderate Democrats, CNN is offering AIPAC a free platform to spread Islamophobia and reinforce the idea that responsible politicians have to support Israel’s genocide, and every person or institution with power and money to the left of Hitler is trying to reinforce the idea that Jeffries and Schumer are the best possible leaders of the Party, in the hopes of preserving a pro-police, pro-deportation, pro-billionaire, pro-AI, pro-Israel agenda.




So what do all these results mean for some important questions? What kinds of changes might we expect from the electoral victories of the Left?




—




Possible







The most recent right-wing wave that has seen governments across the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia shift to the Right may break, at least for now.










More marginalized and lower class populations will probably get access to government-funded resources.




Some workplace protections, environmental regulations, and rights to healthcare will be expanded or restored.




The repression against anticolonial and anticapitalist movements might shift to softer tactics.




The war against Iran might end, for now.







As a low-income person who relies on government assistance for healthcare, with a lethal (but fortunately very slow-moving) cancer caused by environmental toxins, who generally works jobs that involve dangerous or unhealthy conditions and few to no benefits, and who participates in movements constantly subjected to surveillance and repression, and with beloved friends who experience more brutal forms of repression that I don’t, I’m happy for all of these things. They make a difference. But is that difference enough?




—




Not Gonna Happen







We won’t be freed of the obligation to work for bosses in jobs that are often humiliating, unhealthy, and unsafe.




Poverty won’t disappear.




We won’t be allowed to have an unalienated relationship with our homes and the land: housing will continue to be designed as a way to enrich the wealthy and preserve our dependence on them, and land will continue to be treated as property.




Prisons and police won’t disappear, and the routine torture and brutality they produce will continue.




Political repression of anarchists, autonomous movements, and Indigenous communities fighting to get their land back won’t end, and when the Left is in power those facing repression will receive less solidarity and more isolation.




No historical form of oppression like white supremacy or patriarchy will disappear; they will continue to operate through and intensify systemic features like work, poverty, housing, policing, and repression.




Israel will not stop the genocide against Palestinians.




Indigenous peoples around the world will not be allowed to have autonomy over their land and culture.




Governments and corporations from Europe, North America, and South and East Asia will not stop sponsoring wars, genocide, slave labor, and deadly mining and plantation industries across sub-Saharan Africa.




Greenhouse gas emissions reductions will not happen fast enough to avert the acceleration of the worst mass death and mass extinction events in human history. Many years, there will be no emissions reductions at all.




Real emissions reductions, when they do occur, will be based on energy technologies that prioritize economic growth and cause a huge boom in land theft, toxic mining, death squads, and habitat destruction.




Other forms of ecocide and extractivism like industrial agriculture will continue to kill the soil, destroy the forests and wetlands, abuse workers, brutalize hundreds of millions of non-human animals, and drive ongoing land theft and genocide against Indigenous peoples.




The list only continues…







These elections have won us a little bit of breathing room, nothing more. The only way to create the kinds of change we need for survival is through waves of revolution that destroy, abolish, transform, and heal all the vestiges of that trinity of evil – capitalism, colonialism, and the State.




Those three forces are inseparable. They can’t be reformed, and none of them can be abolished while leaving the others intact. Only the State has ever existed without the other two but the emergence of colonial capitalism transformed all the various state models in the world into the modern state, which has proven unable to abolish capitalism no matter how many red flags it waves.




We have an extremely low chance of helping to launch these waves of revolution, sticking to it, adapting, overcoming, and winning, and if we do succeed it’s a labor that requires generations. And yet, it’s a bet we need to take, because there’s a 100% chance of immense suffering and death under the present system. There’s a 0% chance of reforming this system into something good through the methods of change it offers us, like elections. And, of the dozens of authoritarian Left revolutions that have succeeded in their strategy of seizing state power, exactly 0 have abolished capitalism, oppressive hierarchies, poverty, wars, or ecocidal ways of living.




How about we give a chance to the methods and traditions of struggle that have always predicted that would be the outcome of electoral reform or revolutionary states? How about we give a chance to the methods and traditions of struggle that have always rejected colonial society and fought for a world of 

ecocentric communities

 organized through 

rooted networks

 and mutual aid?

title: Giorgio Agamben: Neolithic conservative
content:
Paul Goodman, one of the most radical anarchist thinkers of the twentieth century, once described himself as a “Neolithic conservative”. And Ivan Illich, who believed he had one foot in the Catholic tradition and the other in the mire of his own time, said that his orthodoxy was so ancient and complete as to be revolutionary. This means that to understand and perhaps even to undo the historical era in which we live, we must keep one foot in prehistory. This situation on the threshold or at the boundary between two incommensurable eras is precisely what our age proves incapable of. Not only does it think in a single dimension, but it has lost all connection with its own past, without which any access to the present is impossible. For this reason, it can only look towards a future which, in reality, is nothing but the consequence of a past of which it is totally unaware, and which pulls its strings like a marionette. Only those who stand on two legs between the past and the present can come to terms with both and not be unconsciously determined by them. Only a Neolithic conservative can be revolutionary enough to open up a new space for thought and action.

title: Giorgio Agamben: The countless people
content:
One of the fundamental political problems — if not the most urgent — is how to conceive of an uncountable multiplicity (or multitude). As a political concept, the people only makes sense on condition that it is uncountable; if it can be counted, then what is decisive is no longer the people as such, but a numerical quantity — the so-called majority — into which the people dissolves according to the perverse mechanism of elections or plebiscites. The people—like the human race—are not a collection of countable singularities: the “popular” or “generic” character—that is to say, the political character—must belong entirely to the singular as such. This is what Marx sought to articulate through the concept of 

Gattungswesen

 (“generic being”), which defines each individual and not a countable quantity. title: Giorgio Agamben: Hope and desire
content:
Evelyn De Morgan, “Hope in a Prison of Despair”, 1887







Our condition, in terms of hope and desire, resembles that of those who, in Dante’s 

Divine Comedy

, remain suspended in Limbo and who, in Virgil’s words, desire without any longer hoping (

sanza speme vivemo in disio

). We too, like the inhabitants of Limbo, are suspended between desire and hope: we have lost hope in a better world and yet we continue to desire it in vain and cannot do without it. To emerge from this liminal state, we must direct our hope not towards a good that we lack and wish to possess, but towards that which we already possess, the good that lies within us, so that it may remain alive and give us life. And if faith is, in the words of the Apostle, the assurance of things hoped for [cf. 

Hebrews

 11:1], these things are present within us and before us, and the desire for a good in which we believe is always already fulfilled. Hope in what we have is, therefore, a special form of memory, which is not limited to recalling a past good, but which ceaselessly works to ensure that it remains present and alive. And this transformation of hope into memory is thought, the life of the mind.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Ian Alan Paul: The Disorder of Things
content:
from 

Ill Will

, 22/10/2026







On the final pages of his 

Republic

, Plato presents us with the image of a perfect, total order that no earthly city could ever achieve. Ian Alan Paul’s “The Disorder of Things” begins where Plato’s text leaves off. Yet far from an indictment of earthly life, Paul argues that the imperfection highlighted by Plato does not mark the failure of order but serves as its condition of possibility. This is true existentially as it is politically: just as existence has no essence, no intrinsic form or foundation, political orders operate by ordering a disorder they can never fully extinguish. The state, capital, algorithmic control societies: as these orders attempt to ward off their own inevitable death, they give shape to an increasingly dying world, from ecological collapse to genocide to ever-intensifying security. The task of contemporary political insurgency is to bring about the death of this order.




Order is thus something different than form, which has an anarchic plasticity to it. Anarchy, for Paul, refers to a constitutive non-coincidence of life with itself that serves as the ground of our autonomy, one which order seeks at once to appropriate and to suppress. Whereas order fixes hierarchies among forms, deciding thereby which lives are permissible and which disposable, the form-giving anarchy of existence remains irreducible to it.

Seventy years ago (on 6 May 1898) there was a massive demonstration of workers, men and women, in the centre of Milan. The events which led up to it involve too long a history to treat with here. The demonstration was attacked and broken up by the army under the command of General Beccaris. At noon the cavalry charged the crowd: the unarmed workers tried to make barricades: martial law was declared and for three days the army fought against the unarmed.
